*easily and passively receives, stores, and accumulates (from which all other things flow), if they are flawed, confused, and rashly abstracted from Reality; nor is there any less whim and inconstancy in the secondary and remaining notions. From this it follows, that the whole of that <term>Human Reason</term> <note>original: "Ratio Humana"; the capacity for logical thought and analysis</note> which we employ regarding the <term>Investigation of Nature</term> <note>original: "Inquisitio Naturæ"</note> is not well constructed or built up, but is like some magnificent Structure without a foundation. For while men admire and celebrate the False powers of the Mind, they overlook and lose its True powers (which could exist, if the proper aids were applied to it, and if the mind itself were compliant to Reality, rather than powerlessly insulting it). There remained but one course: that the matter be attempted entirely anew, with better protections; and that there be a universal <term>Restoration</term> <note>original: "Instauratio"; a complete renewal or rebuilding</note> of the Sciences, the Arts, and all Human Learning, raised up from the proper Foundations. Nevertheless, he believed he should not abandon the cause or himself, but should instead attempt and set foot upon the Path which alone is open to the **Human Mind** <note>original: "Humana Mens"</note>. For it is better to provide a Beginning to a matter that can reach a Conclusion, than to be entangled in perpetual strife and study over things that have no end. Furthermore, the **Contemplative Paths** <note>original: "Viae Contemplativae"; methods of theoretical inquiry</note> almost mirror those famous paths of action: where one, steep and difficult at the start, ends in the open; while the other, at first sight easy and downhill, leads into trackless wastes and over cliffs. 

Because he was uncertain when these thoughts might occur to anyone else in the future—guided especially by the fact that he has found no one so far who has applied their mind to similar reflections—he decided to publish whatever first parts he could complete. This haste was not born of ambition, but of concern; so that if anything common to humanity should happen to him <note>a polite euphemism for his own death</note>, there would still exist a certain **Blueprint** and a destination for the Work he has conceived. At the same time, it would stand as a Sign of his honorable and earnest goodwill toward the **Benefit of the Human Race** <note>original: "Generis Humani Commoda"</note>. # OF FRANCIS
#### OF
# VERULAM
### THE GREAT RENEWAL.
### PREFACE.

*On the state of the Sciences: that it is neither prosperous nor greatly advanced; and that a path entirely different from that known to our predecessors must be opened for the human Intellect <note>original: "Intellectui"</note>, and other aids must be provided, so that the mind may exercise its lawful authority over the Nature of things.*

---

<image-desc>Ornate woodcut initial 'V' decorated with scrolling acanthus leaves and floral motifs.</image-desc>
It seems to us that men neither well understand their wealth <note>original: "opes"; referring to the accumulated knowledge of the past</note> nor their strength; but rather believe more than is just concerning the former, and less than is just concerning the latter. Thus it happens that they either value the received arts at insane prices and seek nothing further; or, despising themselves more than is fair, they consume their strength on trivial matters <note>original: "levioribus"</note> and do not test themselves in those things which lead to the core of the matter. Therefore, the Sciences also have their Columns <note>original: "Columnæ"; a reference to the Pillars of Hercules, which in the ancient world marked the boundary of the known world with the warning "nothing further beyond"</note>, as if fixed by fate; since men are moved neither by desire nor by hope to penetrate further. And, since the opinion of plenty is among the greatest causes of poverty; and since from a confidence in present things,

<summary>In this opening of the preface, Bacon argues that human progress is stalled because people either overvalue existing knowledge or lack the confidence to seek new discoveries, effectively creating a self-imposed boundary to science.</summary>
<keywords>Francis Bacon, Great Renewal, Instauratio Magna, scientific progress, Pillars of Hercules, human intellect, philosophy of science</keywords>

### PREFACE.

...true aids may be neglected in the future; it is useful, and plainly necessary, that from those things which have been discovered so far, at the very threshold of our work (and this without ambiguity or concealment), the excess of honor and admiration be removed; with a useful warning, lest men take their abundance or utility for more than they are, or celebrate them as such. For if anyone looks more closely into all that variety of books in which the **Arts** and **Sciences** <note>original: "Artes & Scientiæ"</note> exult, he will find everywhere infinite repetitions of the same thing, differing in the manner of treatment, but already anticipated in their discovery; so that all things, which at first glance seem numerous, are found to be few upon examination.

And concerning utility, it must be stated openly: that **Wisdom** <note>original: "Sapientiam"</note> which we have drawn chiefly from the *Greeks* <note>Bacon refers specifically to the traditional academic philosophy of the universities, largely based on Aristotle, which he found to be more focused on argument than practical results.</note> seems like a certain childhood of **Science**, and possesses what is characteristic of boys: it is ready for chatter, but weak and immature for generating anything. For it is fertile in **Controversies**, but barren of works. So much so that the Fable of *Scylla* <note>In Greek mythology, Scylla was a monster who appeared as a beautiful woman from the waist up, but had barking dogs growing from her womb. Bacon uses this as a metaphor for philosophy that looks beautiful but produces only noise and conflict.</note> seems to fit the current state of letters to the life; she displayed the face and countenance of a virgin, but barking monsters were girt about and clung to her womb. So it is with the Sciences to which we are accustomed: they have certain flattering and showy generalities, but when one comes to particulars—as if to the parts of generation—to bring forth fruit and works from themselves, then contentions and barking disputes arise, which is where they end, and which take the place of offspring. Furthermore, if Sciences of this kind were not plainly a dead thing, it...

<summary>Bacon argues that current knowledge is repetitive and unproductive, famously comparing the Greek philosophical tradition to a talkative child or the monster Scylla—beautiful in appearance but barren and full of noisy disputes.</summary>
<keywords>Scientific Method, Greek Philosophy, Productivity, Scylla metaphor, Scholasticism, stagnation of knowledge</keywords>

### PREFACE.

...her womb; it would least likely have happened—as has been the case for many centuries—that those sciences should remain almost fixed in their tracks, failing to receive any growth worthy of the human race. To such an extent does this occur, that often not only does an assertion remain a mere assertion, but even a question remains a question, and is not resolved through debate, but rather fixed and maintained by it. Every tradition and succession of disciplines merely presents the roles of **Master** <note>original: "Magistri"</note> and **Student** <note>original: "Auditoris"</note>, rather than that of the **Inventor** <note>original: "Inventoris"</note> or someone who adds something exceptional to what has been discovered.

In the **mechanical arts** <note term="mechanical arts">original: "artibus mechanicis." In Bacon's time, this referred to practical crafts, engineering, and technology—fields like printing, gunpowder, or navigation—which he saw as more progressive than university philosophy.</note>, however, we see the opposite occurring. These, as if they were partakers of some vital breath, grow and are perfected daily. In their first authors they usually appear crude, almost burdensome and shapeless; but later they acquire new strengths and a certain usefulness, so much so that the interests and desires of men fail and change sooner than these arts reach their peak and perfection.

**Philosophy** <note>original: "Philosophia"</note>, on the other hand, and the **Intellectual Sciences** <note>original: "Scientiae Intellectuales"</note> are adored and celebrated like statues, but they are not moved forward. Indeed, they sometimes flourish most in their first author and degenerate thereafter. For once men have surrendered themselves and joined in the opinion of one person (like **back-bench senators** <note term="back-bench senators">original: "pedarii Senatores." In the Roman Senate, these were members of lower rank who generally did not speak but voted by walking to one side of the house. Bacon uses this to mock scholars who follow a leader without independent thought.</note>), they no longer add breadth to the sciences themselves, but perform a servile duty in decorating and flanking certain authors.

Nor should anyone suggest that the sciences, growing gradually, finally reached a certain state, and then at last (as if con...

### IV PREFACE.

...having traversed the legitimate spaces <note>original: "profligatis spatiis legitimis"</note>, they have fixed their permanent seats in the works of a few authors. Since nothing better could be found, it remains only for those things already discovered to be adorned and cultivated. 

It would certainly be desirable if this were actually the case. But the truer and more accurate view is that these **enslavements of the Sciences** <note>original: "Scientiarum mancipationes." Bacon uses a legal term for the transfer of property to describe how people "sell" their intellect to old systems.</note> are nothing other than a product of the over-confidence of a few men and the laziness and inertia of the rest. 

For after the **Sciences** <note>original: "Scientiæ"</note> had perhaps been diligently cultivated and handled in their various parts, there then arose someone bold in character, who—well-received and celebrated for providing a concise **Method** <note term="Method">original: "Methodi compendia." Bacon is likely referring to Aristotle, whose systematic "shortcuts" to knowledge became the standard university curriculum, potentially at the expense of deeper inquiry.</note>—established an **Art** <note>original: "Artem"</note> in appearance only, while in reality he corrupted the labors of the ancients. 

Yet this is usually pleasing to those who come after, because of the convenient use of the work and because they are bored and impatient with the prospect of new inquiry. But if anyone is moved by a consensus that is now long-established—as if it were the **judgment of Time**—let him know that he relies on a very deceptive and weak foundation. 

For we do not know for the most part what has been discovered and made public in the **Sciences and Arts** <note>original: "Scientiis & Artibus"</note> across various ages and places; much less do we know what has been attempted by individuals and debated in secret. Therefore, neither the **Births of Time** nor its **Abortions** <note>original: "Temporis Partus, nec Abortus." A famous Baconian metaphor: successful discoveries are "births," while failed or lost ideas are "abortions."</note> are fully recorded in the **Chronicles** <note>original: "Fastis"</note>. 

Nor should we value consensus itself, or its long duration, very highly at all. For however various the types of **Civil Government** <note>original: "Politiarum"</note> may be, there is only one state of the Sciences, and it has always been and will remain "popular" <note>meaning: belonging to the common or average mind, rather than the elite seeker of truth</note>. Among the common people, those doctrines flourish most which are either contentious and pu— <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "pugnacious" or "pugnacis."</note>

<summary>Bacon argues that the perceived "perfection" of ancient philosophy is actually a result of intellectual laziness and a preference for easy shortcuts over rigorous new discovery. He challenges the authority of long-standing tradition, suggesting that "Time" is not a reliable judge of truth.</summary>

<keywords>stagnation of science, intellectual laziness, Aristotle, Method, Births of Time, consensus vs truth, history of science</keywords>

### V PREFACE.

...stubborn, or flashy and empty; such as those that either ensnare or soothe assent. Consequently, the greatest minds <note>original: "ingenia"</note> have undoubtedly suffered violence throughout every age; while men of no common capacity and intellect, nevertheless looking out for their own reputations, have submitted themselves to the judgment of time and the multitude. For this reason, if deeper **Contemplations** <note>original: "arctiores Contemplationes"</note> happened to emerge anywhere, they were immediately tossed about by the winds of common opinion and extinguished. To such an extent that **Time**, like a river, has carried down to us what is light and inflated, but has sunk what is heavy and solid. 

Furthermore, even those authors who have seized a kind of dictatorship in the **Sciences** <note term="Sciences">original: "Scientiis." In the 17th century, this referred to any organized body of knowledge or branch of learning, not just "natural science" in the modern sense.</note> and pronounce upon things with such confidence; yet when they return to themselves in intervals of reflection, they turn to complaints about the subtlety of **Nature** <note>original: "Naturæ"</note>, the hiding places of truth, the obscurity of things, the entanglement of causes, and the infirmity of the human mind. Yet they are not at all more modest in this, since they prefer to blame the common condition of men and things rather than confess anything about themselves. 

Indeed, it is almost a ritual with them that whatever any **Art** <note term="Art">original: "Ars." This refers to a systematic skill or craft, such as Logic, Medicine, or Alchemy.</note> does not reach, they decree that very thing to be impossible according to that same art. Nor can the **Art** be condemned, since it is the Art itself that disputes and judges. Thus, the goal is to ensure that ignorance is even delivered from disgrace. 

And those things which have been handed down and received are roughly in this condition: regarding works, they are sterile and full of questions; in their growth, they are slow and languid; feigning perfection in the whole, but poorly filled in the parts; popular in their selection, and [supported by] autho-

<meta>catchword: ri- (completing "authoribus")</meta>

<summary>Bacon argues that the most profound intellectual works are often lost to time while superficial ones survive, and critiques famous scholars for blaming Nature's complexity rather than their own flawed methods.</summary>
<keywords>Time as a river, intellectual dictatorship, subtlety of nature, human infirmity, sterility of science, Francis Bacon</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the critique of the state of learning. The previous page ended with "sa-" (referring to "artibus" or "arts"), leading into the discussion of how some fields of study are protected by artificial appearances rather than true discovery.</meta>

-># VI PREFACE.<-

...[the] **Arts** <note>original: "artibus"</note> themselves are suspect, and therefore protected and displayed by certain artifices. But those who have decided to experiment for themselves and devote themselves to the **Sciences** <term>Sciences</term> <note>original: "Scientiis." This refers to any organized body of knowledge.</note>, and to extend their boundaries, have neither dared to depart entirely from received opinions nor to seek the very sources of things. Indeed, they think they have achieved something **Great** if they introduce and add something of their own; wisely reflecting that they can maintain modesty in agreeing with tradition and freedom in adding to it.

But while consideration is given to popular opinions and customs, these praised **middle paths** <note>original: "mediocritates"</note> result in great detriment to the **Sciences**. For it is hardly possible to both admire authors and surpass them at the same time. Instead, it happens like water, which does not rise higher than the point from which it first descended. Thus men of this sort amend some things, but advance little; they improve things for the better, but do not grow them for the greater.

Nor, however, have there been lacking those who, with greater daring, took everything as a whole into their own hands. Using the force of their intellect <note>original: "ingenii"</note>, and by overthrowing and destroying what came before, they made a way for themselves and their own **decrees** <note term="Decrees">original: "placitis." In this context, these are dogmatic tenets or philosophical principles.</note>. Yet not much progress has been made through their noise; since they did not strive to enlarge **Philosophy** and the **Arts** in reality and practice, but only to exchange decrees and transfer the kingdom of opinions to themselves. The fruit of this is surely meager, since even among opposite errors, the underlying causes of wandering are almost the same.

Finally, if any have been so minded that—beholden neither to the decrees of others nor their own, but favoring liberty—they desired to seek the truth together with others; these were surely honorable in their intentions, but weak in their effort.

Finally, let them seek the Sciences not with arrogance within the small cells of the human **Intellect** <term>Ingenium</term>, but submissively in the greater world. # THE PLAN
# OF THE WORK.

## IT IS COMPOSED OF
### Six Parts.

First: The Divisions of the Sciences.
Second: The New Tool <note>original: "Novum Organum." This refers to Bacon's new system of logic, intended to replace the "Organon" or traditional logic of Aristotle.</note>, or Directions for the Interpretation of Nature.
Third: The Phenomena of the Universe, or a Natural and Experimental History for the Foundation of Philosophy.
Fourth: The Ladder of the Intellect <note>original: "Scala Intellectus."</note>
Fifth: The Forerunners <note>original: "Prodromi."</note>, or Anticipations of the Second Philosophy.
Sixth: The Second Philosophy, or Active Science.

## THE ARGUMENTS OF EACH PART.

Thus, it should not seem surprising if we sometimes depart from the traditional divisions. For an addition, while it alters the whole, necessarily alters the parts and their sections; the accepted divisions only suit the accepted sum of the Sciences as it exists today.

Regarding those things which we shall note as omitted, we will proceed in such a way that we do not merely propose slight titles and concise arguments for what is lacking. # THE PLAN

...[derived] from the genus of *Logic*; although a great, and indeed immense, difference exists. For even that *common logic* <note>original: "Logica vulgaris". This refers to the traditional Aristotelian logic taught in universities during the 17th century.</note> professes to devise and prepare aids and defenses for the intellect; and in this one point they agree. It differs, however, completely from the *Common Logic*, chiefly in three things: namely, in its very end, its order of demonstration, and its beginnings of inquiry.

For to this Science of ours, the end proposed is that not *Arguments* but *Arts* be found; not things consistent with *Principles*, but the very *Principles* themselves; not *probable Reasons*, but *Designations* and *indications of Works* <note>Bacon emphasizes practical, physical results—"Works"—over mere intellectual agreement or winning an argument.</note>. Thus from a different intention, a different effect follows. In the former, the adversary is conquered and bound by *Disputation*; in the latter, *Nature* is conquered by *Work*.

And with such an end, the nature and Order of the *Demonstrations* themselves agree. In *common Logic*, almost the entire effort is consumed with the *Syllogism* <note>A form of logical argument where a conclusion is reached from two premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal). Bacon argues this is too detached from physical reality.</note>. Of *Induction* truly, the *Logicians* <note>original: "Dialectici". Those who practice dialectics, the formal art of logical debate.</note> seem scarcely to have thought seriously; passing it over with a light mention, and hurrying to the formulas of disputing. But we reject demonstration by *Syllogism*, because it acts too confusedly and lets Nature slip from its hands. For although no one can doubt that things which agree in a middle term <note>The "middle term" is the concept that connects the two premises of a syllogism.</note> also agree with each other (which is of a certain *Mathematical* certainty), nevertheless there is this underlying deception: that the *Syllogism* consists of propositions, propositions consist of words, and words are the tokens and signs of notions. We therefore reject the **Syllogism** <note>A form of reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two given or assumed premises. Bacon believes this method is too far removed from physical reality.</note>; and we do so not only regarding principles (to which even the traditional logicians do not apply it) but also regarding intermediate propositions: which the **Syllogism** certainly draws out and brings forth in some manner, but they are sterile of **Works** <note>Bacon uses the term "Works" to mean practical, scientific applications or inventions.</note>, remote from **Practice**, and plainly incompetent regarding the active part of the **Sciences**. A method of reasoning from specific instances to general principles.</note> throughout, both for the minor propositions and the major. For we consider **Induction** to be that form of demonstration which protects the **Sense**, presses close to **Nature**, and hangs over and almost blends into **Works**.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Therefore, the **Order** of demonstration is also plainly inverted. For until now, it has been the custom to proceed such that one flies from the sense and particulars in the first place to the **most general principles** <note>original: "maxime generalia".</note>, as if to fixed poles around which disputes might turn; from these, the rest are derived through intermediate steps. This is certainly a shortcut, but it is headlong, and a path blocked to **Nature**, though well-suited and prone to **Disputations**. But according to our method, **Axioms** <note>term: Axioms (fundamental principles or rules established through observation)</note> are raised up continuously and step by step, so that only in the final place do we arrive at the **Most General Principles**. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Moreover, the failure of the **Senses** is twofold: for they either fail us, or they deceive us. For first, there are very many things which escape the sense even when it is rightly disposed and in no way hindered; either by the subtlety of the whole body, or the minuteness of the parts, or distance of place, or the slowness or even the speed of motion, or the familiarity of the object, or for other reasons. For the testimony and information of the sense is always according to the **Analogy of Man** <note>original: "ex analogia Hominis". This refers to the idea that humans perceive the world through the limited filter of human biology and psychology.</note>, not according to the **Analogy of the Universe** <note>original: "ex analogia Universi". &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Therefore, so that these things may be met; we have sought out and gathered from all sides aids for the **Senses** with much and faithful service: so that substitutions may be supplied for failings, and rectifications for variations. Therefore, we do not attribute much weight to the immediate and proper perception of the **Sense**. Instead, we bring the matter to this point: that the **Sense** judges only the **Experiment**, while the **Experiment** judges the **Thing** itself. 

For this reason, we believe we have established the **Senses**—from which all knowledge of Nature must be sought, unless one prefers to be mad—as sacred High Priests and skilled Interpreters of their own oracles. Thus, while others may seem to defend and honor the **Sense** as a mere profession, we do so in actual practice. Such are the preparations we make for the light of Nature itself, and for its kindling and introduction. These measures might be sufficient on their own if the human **Intellect** <note>original: "Intellectus"</note> were impartial and like a **blank slate** <note>original: "tabula abrasa". This is the philosophical concept of the mind as a clean surface, like a waxed tablet that has been scraped clean, ready to receive new information without bias.</note>. But since the minds of men are so strangely besieged that no clear and polished surface remains to receive the true rays of Things, it becomes necessary for us to seek a remedy for this problem as well.

The **Idols** <note>original: "Idola". Bacon uses this term to describe the various illusions, biases, and false notions that distort human understanding and prevent us from seeing the world as it truly is.</note> by which the **Mind** is occupied are either **Adventitious** or **Innate**. The **Adventitious** <note>original: "Adscititia"; things added or acquired from the outside.</note> idols have migrated into men's minds either from the doctrines and sects of philosophers or from flawed rules of logic and demonstration. But the **Innate** idols are inherent to the very nature of the **Intellect** itself, which is found to be far more prone to error than the **Sense**. For no matter how much men flatter themselves and fall into admiration of the human mind and

# OF THE WORK
<note>Header: OPERIS.</note>

...almost fall into a state of adoration. One thing is most certain: just as an uneven mirror <note>original: "speculum inæquale"</note> distorts the rays of objects according to its own peculiar shape and curvature, so too does the **Mind**. When the Mind is affected by things through the **Senses**, it fails to represent the nature of things faithfully; instead, in the process of forming and devising its ideas, it mixes its own biased nature with the nature of things.

And while those first two kinds of **Idols** <note>These refer to the "Idols of the Tribe" (common to all humans) and "Idols of the Cave" (individual biases), mentioned on preceding pages.</note> can be uprooted only with great difficulty, these last two <note>The "Idols of the Market-place" (language errors) and "Idols of the Theatre" (false philosophical systems).</note> can be removed in no way at all. All that remains for us is to point them out, so that this treacherous and deceptive power of the **Mind** <note>original: "vis ista Mentis insidiatrix"</note> may be noted and exposed. We must do this lest, after the destruction of old errors, new shoots of error should immediately sprout up from the very "bad health" of the **Mind**'s constitution. If we are not careful, the result would be that errors are not extinguished, but merely exchanged for new ones. On the contrary, we must ensure that it is at last eternally established and fixed that the **Intellect** cannot judge anything unless it uses **Induction** <term>Inductio: the process of reaching a general conclusion by looking at specific, observed examples, rather than relying on abstract logic</term> and its legitimate form.

Therefore, this doctrine concerning the purging of the **Intellect**—intended to make the mind capable of receiving the truth—is completed by three **Refutations** <note>original: "redargutionibus"</note>:
1. The **Refutation of Philosophies** <note>rebutting old, flawed systems of thought like those of Aristotle</note>.
2. The **Refutation of Demonstrations** <note>rebutting the flawed ways people try to prove their arguments</note>.
3. The **Refutation of Native Human Reason** <note>addressing the natural flaws inherent in the human brain</note>.

Once these have been explained, and after it has finally become clear what the nature of **Things** and the nature of the **Mind** actually provide, we believe that we have—with divine goodness acting as the bridesmaid—prepared and adorned the bridal chamber of the **Mind** and the **Universe**. Let the prayer of this **Wedding Song** <note>original: "Epithalamii". This is a poetic metaphor: Bacon views the union of the human mind and the natural world as a sacred marriage.</note> be that from this marriage, a lineage of **Inventions** may be born—a lineage that might, in some part, tame and subdue the hardships and miseries of humanity.

# THE PLAN OF THE WORK
<note>Header: DISTRIBUTIO (The Distribution or Plan of the parts of the work).</note>

->*This is indeed the second part of the Work.*<-

But my intention is not only to point out and fortify the paths, but also to set foot upon them. Therefore, the Third part of the Work embraces the **Phenomena of the Universe**; that is, every kind of Experience and a **Natural History** <term>Naturalis Historia: In Bacon’s time, this referred to a systematic collection of all observed facts, data, and experiments regarding nature, serving as the foundation for scientific theory.</term> of the sort that can serve as a foundation for building Philosophy. For no matter how excellent a method of Proof or form of **Interpreting Nature** <note>original: "Naturam Interpretandi"</note> may be—while it can defend and support the **Mind** against error and failure—it cannot provide or supply the material for knowledge itself. 

Truly, for those whose purpose is not to guess and play the prophet, but to discover and know; and who do not intend to devise mimicries and fables of **Worlds** <note>original: "simiolas et fabulas Mundorum"; Bacon is mocking philosophers who create "toy worlds" or imaginary systems instead of studying the real one.</note>, but to look into the nature of this very true **World** and, as it were, dissect it; everything must be sought from the Things themselves. Neither ingenuity, nor meditation, nor any substitution or compensation of argument can suffice for this labor, investigation, and journey through the world; not even if all the talents of all men were to combine. Therefore, we must either take up this task entirely, or abandon the business forever. For until this very day, the way humans have acted makes it no surprise at all if Nature does not reveal her riches.

For first, the **Information** <note>original: "Informatio"</note> provided by the senses themselves is both deficient and deceptive; **Observation** is careless, inconsistent, and as if left to chance; **Tradition** <note>The passing down of scientific knowledge from past authorities.</note> is empty and based on hearsay; **Practice** is too narrowly focused on immediate results and is slavish; and the power of **Experimentation** is blind, dull, and wandering.

# THE PLAN OF THE WORK

...rugged and steep: finally, **Natural History** is light and destitute; they have gathered a most corrupted material for the intellect for the purposes of **Philosophy** and the **Sciences**. Next, the preposterous subtlety and agitation <note>original: "ventilatio"; this refers to the "tossing around" or public airing of arguments used in Scholastic debates, which Bacon found fruitless.</note> of Argumentation is a remedy attempted too late, when things are clearly beyond hope: it does not restore the business in any way, nor does it separate errors from truth. Therefore, no hope of greater increase and progress lies ahead, except in a certain **Restoration of the Sciences** <note>original: "Instauratio Scientiarum," the namesake of Bacon’s grand project.</note>.

The beginnings of this work must be taken entirely from **Natural History**, and that history must be of a new kind and preparation. For it would be in vain to polish the mirror if the images themselves are lacking: and clearly a suitable Material must be prepared for the **Intellect**, not just faithful protections <note>Bacon refers to his new "Logic" or "Method" as the protections (praesidia) that keep the mind from wandering into error.</note> provided for it. Furthermore, our History (just as our **Logic**) differs from the history currently held in many respects: in its end or purpose; in its very mass and composition; then in its subtlety; and also in its selection and its arrangement in relation to those things which follow.

For first, we propose a **Natural History** that does not so much delight by the variety of its contents, or help by the immediate fruit of **Experiments**, but rather sheds light upon the **Discovery** <note>original: "Inventioni"</note> of causes, and provides the first breast for nurturing **Philosophy**. For although we especially pursue **Works** <term>Works: In Latin, "Opera." These are the practical applications, inventions, or "fruits" of science that improve the human condition.</term> and the active part of the sciences, yet we wait for the time of harvest; we do not attempt to mow the moss or the green, immature crop. For we know well enough that **Axioms** <term>Axioms: The general principles or laws of nature that are discovered through systematic observation (induction).</term> rightly discovered draw whole ranks of **Works** along with them; and works not scattered, but

# THE PLAN

...but to present them in a mass. However, we utterly condemn and cast aside that untimely and childish desire to seize hastily upon some pledges of new **Works**, like the **apple of Atalanta** <note>original: "pomum Atalantæ." In Greek mythology, the huntress Atalanta was distracted during a race by golden apples thrown by her opponent; Bacon uses this to warn against scientists being distracted from the "race" for truth by the temptation of immediate, superficial discoveries.</note>, which delays the race. And such is the duty of our **Natural History**.

Regarding the **Mass** <note>original: "Congeriem"; the physical bulk or collection of information.</note> of it, we are composing a **History** not only of **Nature free and unconstrained** <note>original: "Naturae liberae ac solutae."</note>; (when, that is, she flows of her own accord and performs her own work; such as the History of the **Heavenly Bodies**, **Meteors**, the **Earth** and **Sea**, **Minerals**, **Plants**, and **Animals**:) but much more of **Nature constrained and vexed** <note>original: "Naturae constrictae et vexatae." This is one of Bacon’s most famous concepts: that nature reveals her secrets more clearly when "tortured" or pressured by experimental conditions than when observed in her natural state.</note>; namely, when by human <term>Art</term> <note>meaning technology, craft, or experimental method</note> and service she is forced out of her natural state, and is pressed and molded. 

Therefore, we record all the **Experiments** of the <term>Mechanical Arts</term> <note>In the 17th century, these were the manual trades and crafts, such as smithing or weaving, which Bacon believed held more scientific truth than abstract philosophy.</note>, all those of the operative part of the **Liberal Arts**, and all those of several practical fields which have not yet formed into a proper **Art** (as far as we have been able to investigate, and as far as they serve our purpose). Nay, even (to speak plainly) caring nothing for the pride of men and for showy things, we place much more labor and support in this part than in the other: since the nature of things reveals itself more through the **vexations of Art** than in its own freedom.

Nor do we present a **History** of **Bodies** only; we have also thought it part of our diligence to include the **Virtues** themselves <note>original: "Virtutum." Here, "virtues" refers to the inherent powers, properties, or fundamental forces of matter.</note> (we mean those which might be considered <term>Cardinal</term> <note>fundamental or "hinge" properties</note> in Nature, and in which the first principles of Nature plainly...)

## THE PLAN
<note>original: "DISTRIBUTIO"</note>

...and the superstitions and trifles which nurses instill in children can seriously corrupt their minds. For this same reason, we are moved to be solicitous and even anxious that from the beginning—when we treat and care for the infancy of *Philosophy* <note>In Bacon’s time, "Philosophy" referred to the whole of science and the systematic study of nature.</note> under the form of *Natural History*—it does not become accustomed to any vanity or falsehood. We do this so that, once it has been revealed how each piece of data was established by us, men may see what error might lie beneath or stick to it. They are provided as a pledge to men that they will not be perpetually tossed about in the waves of *History*; and so that, when the work of the *Understanding* <note>original: "Intellectus." ### OF THE WORK.

...[a fourth part] <note>The text begins mid-word, completing "Quartum" (Fourth), referring to the Fourth Part of Bacon's plan.</note> can be made that is safe and convenient for **Nature**, and that sound and prepared **Material** <term>Material (materia): The raw data and observations gathered from nature to be processed by the mind.</term> is provided to the **Understanding**, we judge.

Now that we have fortified the **Understanding** with the most faithful aids and protections, and have gathered a just army of **Divine Works** <note>original: "Divinorum Operum." The first of these is that **Examples** of inquiry and discovery be proposed, represented in certain subjects according to our own method and way. We choose those subjects especially which are both the noblest among those being sought and the most diverse among themselves, so that an **Example** is not lacking in each kind. Nor do we speak of those **Examples** which are added to individual Precepts and Rules for the sake of illustration (for this we have performed abundantly in the Second Part of the Work); but we clearly mean **Types** and **Models** <note>original: "Typos et Plasmata." While it can mean "machine," in 17th-century mathematics it often refers to a visual aid or physical model used to clarify a proof.</note> is present, it is easy and clear to follow the **Demonstration**; on the contrary, without this convenience, everything seems tangled and more subtle than it actually is. <meta>This page continues Bacon’s "Distribution of the Work" (Distributio Operis), where he outlines the six parts of his project. -># THE DISTRIBUTION<-

We have assigned a fourth part to our **Work**; which in truth is nothing else than a particular and detailed application of the **Second Part**.

But the fifth part is used only for a time, until the rest are completed; and it is offered like interest on a loan, until the principal can be collected. For we do not seek our end so blindly that we neglect the useful things that occur along the way. Therefore, we compose the Fifth part of the **Work** from those things which we have either discovered, or proved, or added—not, however, by using the methods and rules of **Interpretation** <term>Interpretation (Interpretandi): Bacon’s specific technical term for his new scientific method, which "interprets" nature rather than just guessing at it.</term>, but by using that same exercise of the **Understanding** which others are commonly accustomed to use in inquiry and discovery. 

For since, from our constant intimacy with **Nature**, we hope for greater things from our **Meditations** than our own natural wit might suggest, these findings can serve as tents pitched along the road, so that the mind, while striving toward more certain truths, may rest in them for a while. Yet we declare in the meantime that we do not wish to be bound by those findings, because they were not discovered or proved by the true form of interpretation.

Indeed, there is no reason for anyone to dread this **suspension of Judgment** <note>original: "Judicii suspensionem." Bacon argues that scientists should hold back from making final conclusions until all evidence is in, a core principle of modern science.</note> in a **Doctrine** which does not simply assert that nothing can be known, but rather that nothing can be known except in a certain order and by a certain path. In the meantime, however, this doctrine establishes certain degrees of **Certainty** for practical use and relief, until the **Mind** may come to rest in the explanation of **Causes**. Nor indeed were those schools of **Philosophers** themselves—who simply held to ***Acatalepsia*** <term>Acatalepsia (from Greek): The philosophical belief that things are inherently "incomprehensible" or that certain knowledge is impossible to achieve.</term>—inferior to those who...

...which usurped the license of pronouncing judgment. Those schools, however, provided no aids to the **Sense** and **Understanding**, as we have done; instead, they simply destroyed belief and authority, which is a far different matter, and almost the opposite. <note>Bacon is contrasting his method with the Ancient Sceptics. The **Sixth** part of our **Work** (which all the others serve and wait upon) at last reveals and proposes that **Philosophy** which is drawn out and established from a legitimate, pure, and rigorous inquiry of the kind we have previously taught and prepared. To complete this last Part and bring it to a conclusion, however, is a task placed both beyond our strengths and beyond our hopes. We provide for it (as we hope) beginnings that are not to be despised; the fortune of the human race will provide the conclusion—one which perhaps men, in this current state of **Things** and **Minds**, cannot easily grasp or measure in their imagination. 

For it is not merely **Contemplative** happiness that is at stake, but truly human affairs and fortunes, and all the power of **Works**. <term>Works (Operum): For Bacon, the goal of science is not just "thinking" (contemplation) but "doing"—creating inventions and technologies that improve the human condition.</term> For **Man**, as the servant and interpreter of **Nature**, performs and understands only as much as he has observed of the order, **Work**, or **Mind** of **Nature**; beyond this, he knows nothing and can do nothing. <note>This is one of Bacon’s most famous axioms. And everything depends on this: if anyone [should turn] the eyes of the **Mind**...

## PREFACE.

But the older Greeks (whose writings are now lost) held a more prudent middle ground between the arrogance of dogmatic claims and the despair of **Acatalepsy** <term>Acatalepsy: From the Greek *akatalepsia*, the philosophical conviction that things are fundamentally incomprehensible or unknowable.</term>. ...the dispositions of minds, so that honor and reverence for the **Ancients** <note>original: "Veteribus"; Bacon refers to the classical Greek and Roman philosophers, particularly Aristotle, who dominated the universities of his time.</note> remain untouched and undiminished, and yet we may accomplish what we have set out to do, and enjoy the fruit of our own modesty. But since our aim is this: that a completely different path be opened to the *Intellect* <note>original: "Intellectui"</note>, one untried and unknown to them, the situation is now changed; partisan zeal and factions cease; and we take on the role of a **guide** <note>original: "indicis"; Bacon views himself not as a superior thinker, but as a signpost pointing toward a new way of investigating nature.</note> only. This is certainly a matter of moderate **authority** <note>original: "authoritatis"</note>, and depends more on a kind of good fortune than on skill or excellence. And this kind of warning pertains to *Persons* <note>original: "Personas"</note>; the other pertains to the *Things* <note>original: "Res"</note> themselves.

Indeed, we are not at all concerned with overthrowing this *Philosophy* <note>original: "Philosophia"</note> which now flourishes, or any other that might exist, whether more refined or more extensive than this one. Nor do we stand in the way of this received philosophy, and others of that kind, from nourishing disputes, adorning *Discourses* <note>original: "Sermones"</note>, and being employed for **professorial duties** <note>original: "professoria munera"; the traditional roles of teaching and academic debate in the Scholastic tradition.</note> and the conveniences of civil life, and...

<summary>Bacon clarifies that he is not competing with the genius of ancient philosophers but is instead proposing a completely new method of inquiry. He allows that traditional philosophy remains useful for education and public debate, even as he seeks to move beyond it.</summary>

...might pertain. <note>original: "pertineant"; completing the thought from the previous page.</note> Nay, we even openly signify and declare that the **Philosophy** <note>original: "Philosophiam"</note> we are introducing will not be very useful for those traditional matters. But if there be any mortal whose heart and care is not merely to cling to what has already been discovered and to use it, but to penetrate to things further beyond; and to overcome **Nature** <note>original: "Naturam"</note>, not by defeating an opponent in argument, but by labor and action; and finally, not to form elegant and probable opinions, but to know with certainty and demonstration; let such people, as true **sons of the sciences** <note>original: "Scientiarum filij"</note>, join themselves with us (if they see fit), so that we may leave behind the outer courts of Nature which countless men have trodden, and a path to her inner chambers may finally be opened. And so that we may be better understood, and so that very thing which we wish...

Then, and only then (if it pleases them), after they have begun to be in control of their own faculties, let them use their own judgment.

## APHORISMS

->Concerning the Interpretation of Nature, and the Kingdom of Man.<-

### APHORISM.

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap 'H' containing floral or foliated scrollwork ornaments.</image-desc>

I. Man, as the servant and interpreter <note>original: "minister & Interpres"</note> of Nature, does and understands only as much as he has observed of the order of Nature, whether by direct experience or by thought; beyond this, he neither knows anything nor can he do anything. <note>This is one of the most famous statements in the history of science. Bacon argues that we are not masters of nature by divine right, but rather students who must learn its rules before we can use them.</note>

II. Neither the bare hand nor the intellect left to itself <note>original: "Intellectus sibi permissus"</note> has much power; results are achieved through instruments and aids, which are as necessary for the understanding as they are for the hand. And just as instruments of the hand either stimulate or guide its movement, so also instruments of the mind <note>original: "instrumenta Mentis"</note> either provide suggestions to the understanding or warn it of dangers. <note>Bacon believes that the human mind is naturally prone to error and needs a "new tool"—a specific method—to keep it on the right track, just as a carpenter needs a ruler or a saw.</note>

III. Human knowledge and human power come to the same thing <note>original: "Scientia & Potentia humana in idem coincidunt"</note>, because ignorance of the cause makes the effect impossible to produce. For Nature is only commanded by obeying her; and that which in contemplation is equivalent to a cause, becomes a rule in operation. <note>This is the source of the famous phrase "knowledge is power." Bacon means that if you want to create a specific result (an "operation"), you must first understand the natural laws (the "cause") that govern it. You cannot "break" the laws of nature; you can only use them by following them perfectly.</note>

<summary>This page marks the beginning of the *Novum Organum*, introducing the first three fundamental aphorisms that define the relationship between human knowledge and the natural world. Bacon argues that humans must act as "interpreters" of nature and that scientific progress requires specific tools and a strict adherence to natural laws.</summary>
<keywords>Francis Bacon, Aphorisms, Nature, Scientific Method, Knowledge is Power, Human Understanding, Natural Law</keywords>

IV. Toward the production of works, Man can do nothing else than move natural bodies toward or away from one another; the rest, Nature accomplishes from within. <note>Bacon suggests that human "invention" is really just the rearranging of physical materials; the actual chemical or biological processes that follow are performed by Nature itself.</note>

The Mechanic, the Mathematician, the Physician, the Alchemist, and the Magician <note>original: "Mechanicus, Mathematicus, Medicus, Alchymista, & Magus"</note> are accustomed to involve themselves with Nature (as far as works are concerned); but all of them, as things now stand, do so with slight effort and slim success. <note>In the 1600s, "Magicians" and "Alchemists" were often considered proto-scientists attempting to manipulate nature, though Bacon critiques them here for lacking a rigorous, successful method.</note>

VII. The productions of Mind and Hand seem quite numerous in books and in manufactures. But all that variety consists in the extreme refinement and the derivations of a few things already known, not in the number of <term>Axioms</term> <note>original: "Axiomatum." In Bacon's work, an "Axiom" is a general principle or law of nature arrived at through systematic observation (induction), rather than a self-evident truth.</note>.

VIII. Even those works which have already been discovered are owed to Chance and Experience more than to the Sciences; for the sciences we now have are nothing more than certain arrangements of things previously discovered, not methods of discovery or designs for new works.

IX. Indeed, the cause and root of almost all evils in the Sciences is this one thing: that while we falsely admire and extol the powers of the human mind, we do not seek its true aids.

X. The subtlety of Nature <note>original: "Subtilitas Naturæ"</note> surpasses the subtlety of Sense and Intellect many times over; so that those beautiful meditations, human speculations, and explanations are unhealthy things, except that there is no one present to notice it. <note>Bacon argues that Nature is far more complex than our minds can imagine. Our theories often look consistent only because we are too ignorant to see where they fail to match reality.</note>

XI. Just as the sciences which we now possess are useless for the discovery of practical works, so also the **Logic** we now possess is useless for the discovery of sciences.

XII. The **Logic** now in use serves more to establish and fix errors (which are founded on common, everyday notions) than to inquire after truth; therefore, it is more harmful than useful.

XIII. The <term>Syllogism</term> <note>A form of reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises, such as: "All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal." Bacon argues this is too rigid for science.</note> is not applied to the first principles of sciences, and is applied in vain to intermediate <term>Axioms</term> <note>General principles or laws of nature.</note>, since it is far from being a match for the subtlety of Nature. It therefore constrains our assent, but not the things themselves. <note>Bacon means that while a syllogism can force us to agree with an argument's logic, it doesn't actually describe or change the physical reality of the world.</note>

XIV. The <term>Syllogism</term> consists of propositions, propositions consist of words, and words are the tokens of notions. Therefore, if the notions themselves (which are the very basis of the matter) are confused and recklessly abstracted from things, there is no stability in what is built upon them. Thus, our only hope lies in true **Induction**. <note>Induction is the method of drawing general conclusions from specific, observed instances, rather than starting with a general rule.</note>

XV. There is nothing sound in our notions, whether in **Logic** or in **Physics**. Neither *Substance*, nor *Quality*, *Action*, *Passion*, nor *Being* itself are sound notions; much less are *Heavy*, *Light*, *Dense*, *Rare*, *Moist*, *Dry*, *Generation*, *Corruption*, *Attraction*, *Repulsion*, *Element*, *Matter*, *Form*, and the like; rather, all of these are fantastical and poorly defined.

XVI. The notions of the lowest species—such as *Man*, *Dog*, *Dove*—and of the immediate perceptions of the senses—such as *Hot*, *Cold*, *White*, *Black*—do not deceive us much; yet even these are sometimes [confused by the] <note>The sentence continues on the next page; the original Latin ends with "a fluxu," suggesting the changing or "flowing" nature of matter.</note>

XVII. XVIII. The things discovered in the **Sciences** so far are of such a kind that they fall almost entirely under common notions. XIX. There are, and can be, only two ways to search for and discover truth. One flies from the senses and particulars to the most general **Axioms**, and from these principles—and their unshaken truth—it judges and discovers intermediate **Axioms**; this way is currently in use. The other way draws **Axioms** from the senses and particulars by climbing steadily and by degrees, so that it reaches the most general principles only at the very end. This is the true way, but it is yet untried.

### NOVUM ORGANUM

...readily point out and designate; therefore they make the sciences active. <note>In Bacon’s view, a "science" is only valuable if it allows us to act upon the world and produce results, rather than just winning an argument.</note>

XXV. The **Axioms** <note>original: *Axiomata*; in this context, these are the fundamental principles or "rules" of a science.</note> currently in use have been derived from meager and hand-picked experience and a few particular instances that occur most frequently; they are generally constructed and expanded to fit the exact measure of those instances. Thus, it is no wonder if they do not lead to new particular instances. If, by chance, some instance offers itself that was not previously noticed or known, the **Axiom** is saved by some frivolous distinction, when it would be more truthful for the principle itself to be corrected.

XXVI. For the sake of teaching, we are accustomed to calling that human reasoning which we apply to Nature as **Anticipations of Nature** (because it is a rash and premature thing), but that reasoning which is elicited from things in the proper ways, we call the **Interpretation of Nature**.

XXVII. **Anticipations** are strong enough to achieve consensus; for even if all men were to go mad in the same way and in a uniform manner, they could agree with one another well enough.

XXVIII. Indeed, **Anticipations** are far more powerful at gaining assent than **Interpretations** are. This is because they are gathered from a few instances—and primarily those which occur familiarly—so they strike the **Understanding** <note>original: *Intellectum*</note> immediately and fill the **Imagination** <note>original: *phantasiam*</note>. On the other hand, **Interpretations** are gathered here and there from things that are quite varied and widely separated; they cannot strike the **Understanding** suddenly. Consequently, in terms of common **Opinions**, they must necessarily seem harsh and discordant—almost like the **Mysteries of Faith**. <note>original: *mysteriorum fidei*; Bacon suggests that true scientific discoveries often sound as strange or unbelievable to the average person as religious miracles or dogmas do, because they contradict our everyday common sense.</note>

### OF VERULAM <note>original: *VERULAMII*; referring to Francis Bacon’s title as Baron Verulam</note>

XXIX. In those Sciences which are founded upon opinions and dogmas, the use of **Anticipations** and **Logic** <note>original: *Dialecticæ*; the formal art of debate and reasoning used in the schools of Bacon's time</note> is appropriate; this is the case when the goal is to overpower an audience's assent, rather than to master the things themselves.

XXX. Not even if the greatest minds of every age were to unite, pooling and passing down their labors, could any great progress be made in the sciences through **Anticipations**. This is because fundamental errors—those made in the mind’s "first digestion" <note>An analogy to the stomach; Bacon suggests that if the initial intake of information is poorly processed, later thinking cannot fix it</note>—cannot be cured by even the most excellent later efforts or remedies.

XXXI. It is in vain to expect any great increase in scientific knowledge by merely layering and grafting new ideas onto the old. Instead, a complete **Restoration** <note>original: *instauratio*; this refers to Bacon's "Great Instauration," his project to rebuild all human knowledge from the ground up</note> must be carried out from the very foundations, unless we are content to spin perpetually in circles, making only meager and almost contemptible progress.

XXXII. The ancient authors retain the honor due to them, as do all others. This is because I am not comparing my own intellect or talents to theirs, but rather comparing our **Methods** <note>original: *viæ*; literally "ways" or "paths"</note>. I do not take on the role of a Judge, but rather that of a Guide <note>original: *Indicis*; one who points the way or provides a signpost</note>.

XXXIII. It must be stated openly: no fair judgment can be made regarding my method, nor the discoveries made using it, by means of **Anticipations** (that is, the type of reasoning currently in use). It is not reasonable to ask that a case be decided by the very system of judgment that is itself being put on trial.

XXXIV. Even the task of teaching or explaining the things I am putting forward is not easy. This is because things which are truly new are still usually interpreted through their resemblance <note>original: *analogia*</note> to the old.

XXXV. **Borgia** <note>Cesare Borgia, the Italian Renaissance statesman and general</note> said of the expedition of the French into **Italy**, that they came with chalk in their hands to mark out their lodgings, rather than with arms to break through. XXXVI. There remains for us but one simple way of teaching: we must lead men to the particulars themselves, and to their Sequences and Orders; and men must, in turn, command themselves for a time to set aside their Notions, and begin to become familiar with things themselves.

XXXVII. <meta>This page continues from page 33, where Bacon concluded that the human mind must be cautioned against the natural errors that obstruct true scientific progress. Here, he begins his famous classification of these errors, which he calls "Idols."</meta>

# VERULAM <note>Referring to Francis Bacon, the 1st Baron Verulam and Viscount St. Alban</note>

...they should fortify themselves against them as far as possible.

**XXXIX.** There are four types of **Idols** <note>original: *Idola*; Bacon uses this term to describe the deep-seated prejudices, illusions, and habitual errors that haunt the human mind and prevent objective understanding</note> that occupy human minds. For the sake of instruction, we have given them names: let the first type be called **Idols of the Tribe** <note>original: *Idola Tribus*</note>; the second, **Idols of the Cave** <note>original: *Idola Specus*</note>; the third, **Idols of the Marketplace** <note>original: *Idola Fori*</note>; and the fourth, **Idols of the Theatre** <note>original: *Idola Theatri*</note>.

**XL.** The formation of Notions and Axioms through **true Induction** <note>original: *Inductionem veram*; a systematic method of reasoning from specific observations to general truths, as opposed to making hasty guesses</note> is certainly the proper remedy for warding off and removing these Idols. Yet, identifying the Idols is also of great use. Indeed, the doctrine of Idols serves the **Interpretation of Nature** <note>original: *Interpretationem Naturæ*</note> in the same way that the doctrine of **Sophistical Refutations** <note>original: *Sophisticis Elenchis*; a reference to Aristotle's work on identifying logical fallacies</note> serves **common logic** <note>original: *Dialecticam vulgarem*</note>.

**XLI.** The **Idols of the Tribe** are rooted in human nature itself, and in the very tribe or race of mankind. For it is falsely asserted that human sense is the measure of all things. On the contrary, all perceptions—of the senses as well as the mind—are based on the **analogy of Man** <note>meaning they are seen through a human lens or perspective</note>, not the **analogy of the Universe**. The **human Intellect** is like an uneven mirror catching the rays of things; it mingles its own nature with the nature of things, distorting and staining it.

**XLII.** The **Idols of the Cave** are the Idols of the individual man. For everyone (besides the errors common to human nature in general) has a certain individual cave or den of his own, which breaks and corrupts the light of Nature; this happens either because of each person’s unique and singular nature, or because of their education and conversation with others;

<summary>In this foundational passage, Bacon introduces his "Four Idols," the mental fallacies that distort human understanding. He specifically defines the Idols of the Tribe (errors inherent to the human species) and the Idols of the Cave (errors unique to individuals).</summary>

...have pleased [the mind], (either because they are accepted and believed, or because they are pleasing), it draws all other things to support and agree with them. LIV. Men fall in love with particular sciences and contemplations; either because they believe themselves to be the authors and inventors of them, or because they have put a great deal of work into them and have become most accustomed to them. Such men, if they turn to philosophy and universal contemplations, twist and corrupt them according to their prior fancies. This is seen most clearly in *Aristotle*, who made his natural philosophy a total slave to his logic, rendering it almost useless and full of contention. Moreover, the tribe of <term>chemists</term> <note>original: *chymicorum*; here referring to alchemists and early chemical practitioners who sought to explain the entire universe through the lens of their furnace experiments.</note>, from a few experiments at the furnace, have built up a fantastic philosophy focused on very little. <meta>The header "VERULAMII" refers to Francis Bacon’s title, Baron Verulam.</meta>

...[for] noting the differences of things; others, for noting the similarities of things. For steady and sharp minds are able to fix their contemplations, and linger, and dwell on every subtlety of differences; while lofty and discursive minds both recognize and bring together even the thinnest and most universal <note>original: *catholicas*; in this context, it refers to general or all-encompassing similarities rather than the religious sense of "catholic."</note> similarities of things. Yet both types of mind easily fall into excess, by grasping at either the degrees of things or their shadows.

**LVI.** Some minds are found to be poured out in admiration of **Antiquity**, others in the love and embrace of **Novelty**; few indeed are of such a temperament that they can hold a middle ground, so as neither to tear up what has been rightly laid down by the **Ancients**, nor to despise what is rightly brought forward by the **New**. This occurs to the great detriment of the sciences and of Philosophy, since these become matters of devotion to Antiquity and Novelty, rather than matters of judgment. **Truth**, however, is not to be sought from the good fortune of any particular time (which is a variable thing), but from the light of **Nature** and **Experience**, which is eternal. Therefore, these devotions must be renounced; and we must see to it that the intellect is not carried away by them into giving its consent.

**LVII.** Contemplations of **Nature**, and of bodies in their simplicity, break and shatter the intellect; while contemplations of Nature, and of bodies in their composition and configuration, stun and loosen the intellect. **LVIII.** Such then should be the contemplative wisdom <note>original: *Prudentia*</note> used in warding off and removing the **Idols of the Cave**, which primarily arise from a dominant interest, from an excess of synthesis and analysis <note>original: *compositionis & divisionis*</note>, from a devotion to certain periods of history, or from a focus on objects either too large or too small. # OF VERULAM
<note>"Verulamii" refers to Francis Bacon's title as Baron Verulam. This header indicates the author of the work.</note>

[...if one] wishes to shift those lines so that they are more in accordance with nature, words stand in the way <note>original: *verba obstrepunt*; literally "words shout against us" or "obstruct."</note>. Hence it happens that the great and formal disputes of learned men often end in controversies about words and names; it would be more advisable (according to the custom and wisdom of mathematicians) to begin with these, and to bring them into order through definitions. Yet such definitions, in natural and material matters, cannot cure this evil, since the definitions themselves consist of words, and words give birth to words. Thus, it is necessary to return to particular instances <term>particular instances: specific, observable examples in nature as opposed to abstract theories</term> and their sequences and orders, as we shall soon explain when we arrive at the method and logic for establishing Notions and Axioms.

**LX.** The **Idols** which are imposed upon the Intellect through words are of two kinds. They are either names of things that do not exist (for just as there are things that lack a name because they have not been observed, there are also names that lack a physical reality because of an imaginary supposition); or they are names of things that *do* exist, but are confused, poorly defined, and rashly or unevenly abstracted from the objects themselves. Of the first kind are **Fortune**, the **Prime Mover** <note>original: *Primum Mobile*; in ancient and medieval astronomy, the outermost sphere of the heavens that moved all the others.</note>, the **Orbs of the Planets**, the **Element of Fire** <note>Bacon frequently criticized the traditional Greek belief that "fire" existed as a distinct physical sphere or pure element above the atmosphere.</note>, and similar fictions which originate from vain and false theories. This kind of Idol is more easily cast out, because they can be exterminated by the steady rejection and obsolescence of the theories themselves.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Idols of the Market" (Idola Fori). # NOVUM ORGANUM.

But the other kind is complex and deeply rooted, arising from a poor and unskillful process of **abstraction** <term>abstraction: the mental process of forming a general idea by pulling away specific details from many different objects</term>. For example, let us take a certain word—**Humid** <note>original: *Humidum*</note>, if you like—and see how well the things signified by this word agree with one another. It will be found that this word, **Humid**, is nothing more than a confused sign for a variety of different actions that cannot be reduced to any consistent meaning. 

For it is used to mean: 
1. That which easily spreads itself around another body; 
2. That which is in itself indeterminate and cannot stand still; 
3. That which yields easily in every direction; 
4. That which easily divides and scatters; 
5. That which easily unites and gathers together; 
6. That which flows easily and is put into motion; 
7. That which easily sticks to another body and makes it wet; 
8. And that which is easily reduced to a liquid, or melted, when it was previously solid. 

Therefore, when we come to apply and use this name, we find contradictions: if you take it one way, a flame is "humid"; if another way, air is *not* "humid"; if another, fine dust is "humid"; if yet another, glass is "humid." Thus, it becomes clear that this **Notion** <note>original: *Notionem*; a general concept or idea formed in the mind</note> was rashly abstracted from water and common, ordinary liquids alone, without any proper verification.

Among words, however, there are certain degrees of defect and error. The least faulty kind consists of the names of specific substances, especially those of the **lowest species** <note>original: *specierum infimarum*; the most specific categories in a classification system, such as a specific type of plant rather than "plants" in general</note> which have been well-derived. For example, the notions of **chalk** and **mud** are good, while the notion of **earth** is bad.

But faulty demonstrations are like the fortifications and defenses of the *Idols*; and those which we have in *Dialectics* <term>Dialectics: The traditional logic of the time, largely based on Aristotle, which Bacon believed was better suited for debate than for discovering scientific truth.</term> almost entirely result in the *World* being made a slave to human thoughts, and thoughts to words. For *Demonstrations* are themselves, in a certain *Power*, the very *Philosophy* and *Science*. For such as they are, and according as they are rightly or wrongly established, such are the *Philosophies* and *Contemplations* that follow. However, those [demonstrations] which we use in that whole process which leads from the senses and things to *Axioms* and *Conclusions* are deceptive and incompetent. This *Process* is indeed fourfold, and its faults are just as many.

*First*, the impressions of the sense itself are faulty; for the sense both fails and deceives. But failures must be answered with substitutions, and deceptions with rectifications. *Second*, *Notions* are badly abstracted from the impressions of the senses; and they are indeterminate and confused, whereas they ought to be well-defined and clearly bounded. *Third*, *Induction* is bad which concludes the *Principles* of the Sciences by simple enumeration <note>original: "per enumerationem simplicem"; a logical error where one draws a general conclusion from a few instances without considering counter-examples.</note>, without employing the exclusions and resolutions, or the separations of *Nature*, that are required. *Lastly*, that method of discovery and proof, where first...

### LXX.
But by far the best demonstration is **Experience**; provided it remains focused on the experiment itself. For if it is transferred to other things that are thought to be similar, it is a deceptive thing unless that transfer is performed properly and in an orderly way. However, the manner of experimenting that men currently use is blind and stupid. And so, since they wander and stray without any certain path, but take counsel only from the chance meeting of things, they are carried around to many objects but advance very little; sometimes they are excited, sometimes they are distracted; and they always find something further to seek. 

It almost always happens that men experiment lightly and as if in play, by slightly varying experiments already known; and, if the result does not succeed, they become disgusted and abandon the effort. But even if they apply themselves to **Experiments** more seriously, constantly, and laboriously, they still spend their labor in extracting some one particular result; just as *Gilbert* <note>William Gilbert (1544–1603), an English physician and scientist who published "De Magnete," a pioneering work on magnetism.</note> did with the Magnet, or the **Chemists** <term>Chemists: Here Bacon refers to alchemists, who were often criticized for focusing narrowly on the transmutation of gold rather than broader natural laws.</term> did with gold. Men do this with a design that is no less unskillful than it is narrow. For no one successfully searches out the nature of any thing in the thing itself; rather, the inquiry must be expanded to more general principles.

### LXXI.

The sciences we possess have flowed almost entirely from the Greeks. For what Roman writers, or Arabs, or more recent authors have added is neither much nor of great weight; and whatever it may be, it is built upon the foundation of what was discovered by the Greeks. However, the wisdom of the Greeks was "professorial" <term>Professorial: Bacon uses the Latin "professoria" to describe a style of learning designed for public lecturing and academic debate rather than the active, quiet investigation of nature.</term> and prone to overflowing into disputes—a style that is most hostile to the investigation of truth. The only difference was this: the former group was wandering and mercenary, running from city to city, showing off their wisdom and demanding pay; while the latter group was more formal and dignified, being those who had fixed locations, opened schools, and practiced philosophy without charge. Yet both types (though different in other respects) were "professorial" in nature; they reduced every matter to disputes, and...

**LXXII.**
Nor are the Signs much better which can be gathered from the nature of the **Time** and **Age**, than those from the nature of the **Place** and **Nation**. For the knowledge of that age, whether of Time or of the World, was narrow and thin; which is by far the worst condition, especially for those who base everything on **Experience**. Much less did they know the provinces of the **New World**, not even by hearsay or any certain and steady rumor. In fact, many climates and zones, in which infinite peoples breathe and live, were pronounced by them to be uninhabitable. Moreover, the travels of ***Democritus***, ***Plato***, and ***Pythagoras***—though celebrated as something great—were not truly far-reaching, but rather local <note>original: "suburbanae." ### LXXIV.

Signs must also be taken from the growth and progress of Philosophies and Sciences. For those things founded on Nature grow and increase; but those founded on Opinion change, but do not grow. Thus, if those doctrines had not been plainly like a plant torn up by its roots, but had clung to the womb of Nature and been nourished by her, that which we have seen happening for two thousand years would never have occurred: namely, that the sciences remain stuck in their own tracks and stay in almost the same state, without taking on any noteworthy increase; rather, they flourished most under their first author and thereafter declined.

### LXXV.

Yet another **Sign** is to be taken (if indeed the name "Sign" is appropriate here, since it is more of a **Testimony**, and the most powerful of all testimonies): namely, the **own confession of the Authors** whom men currently follow. For even those who pronounce judgment on things with such great confidence still, at intervals when they return to themselves, turn to complaints about the <term>subtlety of Nature</term> <note>original: "Naturæ ſubtilitate." Nor should that **Sign** be overlooked: the fact that there was once such great dissension among Philosophers and such a variety of the Schools themselves. **LXXVIII.** Now, however, we must come to the **Causes of errors**, and to the reasons for such a long delay in them through so many centuries. This is a famous Baconian sentiment: truth is revealed by the passing of time and the accumulation of data, not just by individual brilliance.</note> rather than the offspring of Genius.

**LXXIX.** In the second place, a cause presents itself that is certainly of great importance in every respect: namely, that during those very ages in which human wits and letters flourished most, or even moderately, **Natural Philosophy** <term>Naturalis Philosophia</term> <note>At this time, "Natural Philosophy" was the term for what we now call "Science"—the study of the physical world and its laws.</note> received the smallest portion of human labor. Therefore, since during those three periods Natural Philosophy was greatly neglected or hindered, it is no wonder that men have made so little progress in that field, since they were entirely occupied with other matters.

### LXXXIII.

In **Superstitious Magic** <term>Superstitiosa Magia</term> (if something must be said of this as well), it should especially be noted that there are only certain and definite kinds of subjects in which these curious and superstitious Arts, throughout all Nations, ages, and even religions, have been able to achieve anything. Therefore, let us set those aside. Meanwhile, it is no wonder if the **opinion of Plenty** <term>Copia</term> has been the cause of **Poverty** <term>Inopia</term> <note>original: "si opinio Copiæ, causam Inopiæ dederit." This is one of Bacon's most famous aphorisms: believing we already have all the answers (plenty) prevents us from doing the hard work of discovery, leaving us poor in actual knowledge.</note>.

### NEW ORGANON. ###

For first, in all the **Arts** <term>Ars; refers here to both technical crafts and organized bodies of knowledge</term>, we find a certain caution that has now become familiar: the Authors of any given Art turn the weakness of their own skill into a slander against **Nature**. Whatever their own Art does not achieve, they pronounce—on the authority of that same Art—to be impossible in Nature. Certainly, an Art cannot be condemned if it is allowed to be the judge in its own case. Even the **Philosophy** <term>Philosophia</term> which is now in our hands cherishes in its bosom certain established decrees or dogmas which (if examined more carefully) seek to fully persuade men of this: that nothing arduous, or powerful and commanding over Nature, should be expected from any Art or human work. We see this in the ideas concerning the *Heterogeneity of Heat* <note>original: "Heterogenia Caloris." This refers to the chemical or physical combining of elements.</note>, as was mentioned above.

If these things are observed more accurately, they pertain entirely to a malicious limitation of human power, and to a deliberate and artificial despair. Such despair does not only disturb the omens of hope but also cuts the hamstrings and stimuli of all industry, and even throws away the "dice" of **Experience** <term>Experientia</term> itself. All this is done because these authors are only concerned with ensuring that their own Art is deemed perfect—devoting their efforts to a most vain and ruinous kind of glory. They want it to be believed that whatever has not yet been discovered or understood is entirely impossible to ever be discovered or understood in the future.
