### LXXXIX.
Nor should we overlook the fact that **Natural Philosophy** <note>original: "Philosophia Naturalis"</note> has, throughout all ages, encountered a troublesome and difficult adversary: namely, **Superstition**, and a blind and immoderate zeal for **Religion**. Nor were those of the ancient **Fathers of the Christian Religion** <note>original: "Patrum Religionis Christianæ"</note> much more welcoming to those who, based on most certain demonstrations (which no sane person today would contradict), posited that the **Earth is round**, and consequently asserted that there are **Antipodes** <term>Antipodæ; refers to people living on the opposite side of the globe, whose feet would be "opposite" to ours</term>.

For these men, having reduced **Theology** (as far as lay in their power) to order and molded it into the form of an **Art**, have additionally brought it about that the contentious and thorny ***Philosophy of Aristotle*** <note>original: "Aristotelis Philosophia"</note> should be blended into the body of Religion more than was fitting.

To the same end (though in a different manner) tend the commentaries of those who have not [hesitated] to derive and confirm the truth of the **Christian Religion** from the principles and authorities of **Philosophers**...

## XCII.

But by far the greatest obstacle to the progress of the **Sciences**, and to the undertaking of new tasks and provinces within them, is found in the despair of men and the assumption of the **Impossible**. For even prudent and serious men are accustomed to distrust matters of this kind entirely: they reflect upon the obscurity of **Nature**, the brevity of life, the fallacies of the senses, the weakness of judgment, the difficulties of experiments, and similar things. Thus, they believe that there are certain ebbs and flows <note>original: "fluxus & refluxus"; a tidal metaphor suggesting that knowledge does not move forward in a straight line but merely circles back on itself</note> of the **Sciences** through the **revolutions** <term>revolutions: Here meaning the cyclical movements of time and history, much like the orbits of planets</term> of times and ages of the **World**; that at some times they grow and flourish, and at others they decline and lie dormant; yet in such a way that when they have reached a certain degree and state, they can go no further.

Therefore, if anyone believes or promises greater things, they think it is the mark of an unbridled and immature mind; and that efforts of this kind have, naturally, joyful beginnings, arduous middle stages, and confused endings. ### XCIII.
The beginning, however, must be taken from **God**: for surely this work being done, because of the excellent nature of the Good within it, is manifestly from God, who is the *Author of Good* and the *Father of lights*. <note>original: "Pater luminum"; a reference to the Epistle of James 1:17, implying God is the source of all intellectual and spiritual insight.</note> In divine operations, even the smallest beginnings lead surely to their end. And what was said of spiritual things—*The Kingdom of God does not come with observation* <note>original: "Regnum Dei non venit cum observatione"; from Luke 17:20. Bacon suggests that significant shifts in human history often happen quietly and unnoticed by the masses.</note>—is also found to happen in every major work of divine Providence: so that all things flow along peacefully without noise or sound, and the thing is fully underway before men think or notice it is being done. Nor should the prophecy of **Daniel** <note>Daniel 12:4. ...of the past, and of the paths tried until now. The logic is that failure is encouraging if it was caused by avoidable mistakes.</note> 

In a similar way, if men for such great spans of years had held the true power of discovering and cultivating the **Sciences**, and yet had not been able to advance further, it would undoubtedly be a bold and reckless opinion to believe the matter could be carried any further. 

But if there has been an error in the path itself, and the labor of men has been consumed in things where it was least appropriate, it follows from this that the difficulty does not arise in the **Things themselves**—which are not within our power—but in the **human Intellect**, and its use and application; a matter which admits of remedy and medicine. 

Therefore, it would be best to set forth those very errors: for however many obstacles there were from errors in the past, so many are the arguments for hope in the future. Although these matters were not entirely untouched in what was said above, it nonetheless seemed right to represent them again now briefly, in naked and simple words.

**XCV.** Those who have handled the sciences have been either **Empirics** or **Dogmatists**. The **Empirics**, like ants, merely collect and use; the **Rationalists**, like spiders, spin webs out of themselves. But the way of the **bee** is the middle path: it draws material from the flowers of the garden and the field, but then transforms and digests it by its own power. The true labor of **Philosophy** is not unlike this; for it does not rely solely or even chiefly on the powers of the **Mind**, nor does it take the material provided by **Natural History** and **Mechanical Experiments** and store it in the **Memory** exactly as it was found, but rather stores it in the **Intellect** altered and processed. For the lowest axioms differ very little from bare **Experience**. But those highest and most general axioms (which are currently held) are merely notional and abstract, and they possess no solidity. It is the **Middle Axioms** that are the true, solid, and living principles upon which human affairs and fortunes depend. Above these, eventually, are the truly general axioms; however, these are not abstract, but are instead truly limited and defined by those middle principles.

Therefore, we must not add **wings** to the human **Intellect**, but rather **lead** and **weights**, to restrain every jump and flight. This has not yet been done; but when it is finally done...

**CV.** <note>Aphorism 105</note> In establishing an <term>Axiom</term><note>In Bacon’s method, an "Axiom" is a general law of nature derived from systematic observation, rather than a self-evident logical truth.</note>, however, a different form of *Induction* than the one used until now must be devised; and this must be applied not only to proving and discovering "Principles" (as they are called), but also to the minor, the middle, and finally all axioms. For the *Induction* that proceeds by simple enumeration <note>original: "enumerationem simplicem"; the traditional method of gathering only examples that support a conclusion while ignoring counter-evidence.</note> is a childish thing; it concludes precariously and is exposed to danger from a contradictory instance; it usually pronounces judgment based on fewer facts than is proper, and only those which are close at hand.

But the *Induction* which will be useful for the discovery and demonstration of **Sciences** and **Arts** must separate Nature through proper rejections and exclusions; and then, after a sufficient number of negatives, conclude upon the affirmatives. This has not yet been done, nor even truly attempted, except perhaps by **Plato**, who certainly uses this form of *Induction* to some extent for examining definitions and ideas. But for the good and legitimate instruction of this *Induction*, or *Demonstration*, very many things must be employed which have not yet entered the mind of any mortal; so much so that more effort must be spent on it than has been spent on the *Syllogism* <note>Traditional Aristotelian logic, which Bacon argues is useful for debate but useless for scientific discovery.</note>. And the help of this *Induction* must be used not only for discovering <term>Axioms</term>, but also for defining <term>Notions</term> <note>The basic mental categories or concepts we use to describe the world, such as "heat," "weight," or "matter."</note>. And in this *Induction*, certainly, the greatest hope is placed.

**CVI.** In establishing <term>Axioms</term><note>General laws or principles derived from observation.</note> through this form of *Induction*, we must also perform an examination and a test: we must see whether the Axiom being established is merely adapted and "made to measure" for those specific facts from which it was drawn, or whether it is more extensive and wider in scope. # OF VERULAM

...through supportive measures, far more things must necessarily be discovered. ...driven by multiplying their force, they would have thought many and varied things to themselves. But concerning a **fiery wind** <note>original: "vento igneo"; a reference to the explosive gases produced by gunpowder.</note>, expanding so suddenly and violently and blowing outward, hardly anything would have ever occurred to anyone’s imagination or <term>fancy</term><note>original: "phantasiae"; the mental faculty that constructs images based on past sensory experience.</note>; for they would not have seen a nearby example of it, except perhaps in an earthquake or lightning. These, however, being <term>Great Works of Nature</term><note>original: "Magnalia Naturae"; extraordinary natural phenomena that seem beyond human capability to replicate.</note> and not things that can be imitated by man, people would have immediately rejected the possibility of such an invention.

In the same way, if before the invention of **silk thread** <note>original: "fili bombycini"</note>, someone had introduced a conversation of this kind: "A certain kind of thread has been discovered for the use of clothing and furniture which far surpasses linen or wool thread in fineness, and yet also in strength, and even in luster and softness." People would have immediately begun to form opinions either about some kind of vegetable silk, or about the more delicate hairs of some animal, or about the feathers and down of birds. But they certainly would never have imagined a fabric woven by a tiny worm, produced so copiously, renewing itself, and appearing annually. Indeed, if anyone had even dropped a hint about a "worm," he would surely have been an object of mockery, as one who dreamed of some new way of using spiders' webs.

Similarly, if before the invention of the **Nautical Needle** <note>original: "Acus Nauticae"; the magnetic compass needle.</note>, someone had brought forward a report of this kind: "A certain instrument has been invented by which the <term>Poles</term><note>original: "Cardines"; literally "hinges," referring to the celestial poles or the cardinal points of the compass.</note> and points of the heavens can be exactly grasped and distinguished," people would have immediately begun to talk about more exquisite constructions of astronomical instruments...

...they would have wandered through many and various thoughts by the agitation of their <term>imagination</term><note>original: "phantasiae"; the mental faculty that constructs images based on past sensory experience.</note>. But that something could be found whose motion agreed so well with the heavenly bodies, and yet was not itself of the heavens, but merely a stony or metallic substance <note>Bacon is referring to the magnetic compass needle and its alignment with the poles.</note>, would have seemed entirely incredible. And yet these things, and similar ones, lay hidden from men through so many ages of the world, and were not found through **Philosophy** or the <term>rational Arts</term><note>original: "Artes rationales"; the traditional methods of logic and deduction used in schools at the time.</note>, but by chance and by opportunity. They are of that kind (as we have said) that are plainly <term>heterogeneous</term><note>original: "heterogenea"; meaning "different in kind" or completely unlike existing categories of objects.</note> and most remote from those things known before, so that any prior notion could have contributed nothing at all to them.

Therefore, it is altogether to be hoped that there are still many things of excellent use hidden in the lap of **Nature**, which have no kinship or resemblance to what has already been discovered, but are situated entirely outside the paths of the imagination; which, however, have not yet been found. Without doubt, through many circuits and windings of centuries, these too will eventually come forth on their own, just as those previous ones did; but by the way <note>referring to Bacon's new scientific method</note> we are now treating, they can be represented and anticipated quickly, suddenly, and all at once.

...discoveries of a similar kind might seem to rely on certain properties of Things and Nature; but certainly the art of **Printing** <note>original: "Imprimendi artificium"</note> contains nothing that is not open and almost obvious. In this course of Discovery, the **human Mind** <note>original: "Mens humana"</note> is often so clumsy and poorly disposed that at first it distrusts the possibility, and shortly after, it despises itself. First, it seems incredible to the mind that any such thing could be found; but after it has been found, it seems incredible again that men could have missed it for so long. And this very fact is rightly turned toward **Hope**; namely, that there surely remains a great heap of Inventions yet to be uncovered. These may be derived not only from digging up unknown operations, but also from transferring, combining, and applying those already known, through what we have called **Literate Experience** <term>Experientiam literatam</term> <note>Bacon's term for a systematic, written method of organizing experiments, moving from one experiment to another in a structured way rather than by random chance.</note>.

### LORD VERULAM

...the expense of talent, time, and resources which men bestow on matters and studies of far less use and value; of which if even a small portion were turned to sound and solid things, there is no difficulty that could not be overcome. ### CXII.
In the meantime, let no one be frightened by the multitude of particulars; rather, let this very fact restore **Hope**. For the particular **Phenomena** <note>original: "Phænomena"; the observable facts, events, or circumstances in nature</note> of the Arts and of Nature are like a mere handful compared to the fictions of the mind, once they have been separated and abstracted from the evidence of things. The exit of this path is in the open and is almost within reach; the other path has no exit, but only infinite entanglement. For men have so far spent very little time on **Experience** <note>original: "Experientia"; here meaning the direct observation of nature rather than reading old books</note>, and have only lightly brushed over it, while they have wasted infinite time in the meditations and commentaries of the intellect. If, however, there were someone available who could answer questions about the facts of Nature, the **Discovery of Causes** <note>original: "Inventio Causarum"</note> and of all **Sciences** <note>original: "Scientiarum"</note> would be the work of only a few years.

### CXIII.

# NOVUM ORGANUM. 107

...very much occupied with business, and not of very firm health (which involves a great loss of time), and in this matter clearly a **pioneer** <note>original: "Protopirum"; a term derived from Greek meaning a first-trier or one who makes the first attempt</note>, following in no one’s footsteps, nor even communicating these things with any other mortal; and yet, having constantly entered upon the true way and submitting his mind to the facts, he has (as we judge) advanced these matters to some extent. ### CXIV.
Finally, even if a much weaker and more obscure breeze of **Hope** blew from that **New Continent** <note>original: "nova Continente"; Bacon frequently uses the metaphor of the Age of Discovery to describe the new world of scientific knowledge</note>, we have nevertheless determined that the attempt must absolutely be made (unless we wish to be completely dejected in spirit). For the risk of not trying a thing is not equal to the risk of failing at it; in the former, a great good is at stake; in the latter, only a small loss of human labor is involved. But from what has been said, and even from what has not been said, it seems to us that there is more than enough hope, not only for a man who is energetic in trying, but even for one who is prudent and sober in believing.

### CXVI.

First, therefore, it seems necessary to request that people do not think we wish to found some new sect in Philosophy, after the manner of the Ancient Greeks or certain modern men—such as **Telesio**, **Patrizi**, or **Severinus** <note>original: "Telesii, Patricii, Severini"; these were 16th-century thinkers who, like Bacon, challenged Aristotle, but whom Bacon critiques for merely creating new speculative systems rather than focusing on experimental data</note>. ### CXVII.

And just as I am not the founder of a Sect; so too I am not a giver or promiser of particular works <note>original: "operum particularium"; here "works" refers to specific inventions or practical results</note>. **CXIX.** There will also appear in our **History** and **Experiments** many things: first, those that are trivial and common; second, those that are base and undignified; and finally, those that are too subtle and merely speculative, appearing to be of no use. We are not dedicating or building some **Capitol** or **Pyramid** to the pride of men, but are founding a holy **Temple** in the human intellect after the model of the **World** <note>Bacon contrasts vanity projects like pyramids with the humble, truthful study of God's creation</note>. But enough has been said of this, since this kind of fastidiousness is plainly childish and effeminate.

**CXXI.** But this other point must be examined much more accurately: namely, that many things in our **History** will seem to the common grasp, or even to any intellect (accustomed to the current state of things), to be of a certain curious and useless subtlety. Therefore, concerning this, above all else, something has been said and must be said again. It is this: that for now, at the beginning and for a time, we seek only **light-bearing Experiments** <term>original: "lucifera Experimenta"; experiments that provide discovery and understanding</term>, not **fruit-bearing** ones <term>original: "fructifera"; experiments that provide immediate practical or financial gain</term>. We do this after the example of the **Divine Creation** <note>original: "Creatio divina"</note>, which, as we have often remarked, produced only light on the first day, and assigned one whole day to that alone, without mixing in any material work on that day.

Therefore, if anyone thinks that such things are of no use...

But if anyone is offended by these speculative **Subtleties** <note>Bacon refers here to the minute, detailed observations required by his method</note>; what should be said of the **Scholastics** <term>original: "Scholastici"; medieval philosophers and theologians who focused on logic and the interpretation of traditional texts rather than physical experimentation</term>, who indulged in subtleties to an immense degree? They were not of the kind that had no utility for the present but an infinite utility in the consequence; such as those of which we speak. ### CXXII.

There also occurs this thought: it seems a wonderful and harsh thing that we should set aside all Sciences and all Authors at once, as if with a single blow and impulse; and that we do so without taking any of the **Ancients** <note>The classical philosophers, particularly Aristotle and the Greeks</note> for our aid and protection, but as if by our own strength.

But we know that if we had wished to act with less sincerity, it would not have been difficult for us to refer these things which are proposed either to the ancient ages before the times of the Greeks (when the Sciences of Nature perhaps flourished more, though with greater silence; and had not yet fallen into the trumpets and pipes <note>Bacon often compares Greek philosophy to "trumpets and pipes" because he felt it was designed for public display and noisy disputation rather than practical utility</note> of the Greeks...

<meta>This page continues from page 116, where Bacon concludes his defense of studying "vile" or "common" things. He is now addressing the potential criticism that his "New Tool" (Novum Organum) completely disregards the authority of ancient Greek and Roman philosophers.</meta>

<page-num>117</page-num>
<header>NEW INSTRUMENT <note>original: "NOVUM ORGANUM"</note></header>

...had hitherto occurred) or even to attribute them (at least in part) to some of the *Greeks* themselves, and to seek endorsement and honor from that source: in the manner of "new men" <note>original: "novorum hominum"; a Roman term for parvenus—people who have recently gained wealth or status and try to fake a noble family tree to fit in</note>, who construct and fabricate a nobility for themselves out of some ancient lineage by the grace of genealogies. Nor do we think it matters more to the business at hand whether the things now being discovered were once known to the *Ancients* and have merely set and risen again through the cycles of time and the passing of centuries, than it should be a concern to men whether the *New World* <note>The Americas</note> was that *Island of Atlantis* <note>The legendary lost continent mentioned by Plato; Bacon argues it doesn't matter if the "new" discovery was actually known to the ancients, as the discovery itself is what counts</note> and known to the old *World*, or whether it is only now discovered for the first time. For the discovery of things must be sought from the light of *Nature*, not brought back from the shadows of *Antiquity*.

As for that universal censure <note>Bacon refers to his sweeping rejection of all previous philosophical schools</note>, it is most certain to anyone truly considering the matter that such a critique is both more probable and more modest than if it had been done only in part. For if errors had not been rooted in the first **Notions** <term>original: "Notionibus"; the basic mental categories or concepts, such as "weight," "density," or "element," which Bacon believed were poorly defined by previous philosophers</term>, it would have been impossible for some things to be correctly discovered without them correcting other things discovered wrongly. But since the errors were fundamental, and of such a kind that men simply neglected or passed over facts rather than making a corrupt or false judgment about them, it is not at all surprising if men did not obtain what they did not seek, nor reached the goal they did not set, nor completed the journey they never actually began.

Moreover, what we are saying here applies not only to this, our first and initial attempt, but also to those who will dedicate themselves to this work in the future. For our way of **Discovering the Sciences** <note>original: "Inveniendi Scientias"</note> almost levels the playing field for human intellects, leaving very little to individual brilliance; this is because it carries out everything through the most certain **Rules** <note>original: "Regulas"</note> and **Demonstrations** <note>original: "Demonstrationes"</note>. Therefore, these findings of ours (as we have often said) are the result of a certain good fortune rather than natural ability, and are more the "birth of Time" than the product of genius. For there is surely an element of chance in human thoughts, just as much as there is in our works and deeds.

# NOVUM ORGANUM.

...will respond. For we ourselves acknowledge the ***method of inquiry and discovery*** <note>original: "Formam enim inquirendi & inveniendi"</note> used among the ***Ancients***, and their own writings display it. However, that method was nothing other than to fly from certain ***Examples*** and ***Particulars*** <note>specific observations or individual facts</note> (adding common ***Notions***, and perhaps some portion of the received opinions which pleased them most) toward the most general ***Conclusions*** or ***Principles of the Sciences***. To the unmovable and fixed truth of these principles, they then derived and proved lower ***Conclusions*** through ***Intermediate steps*** <note>original: "Media"; the middle ground of logic between a specific fact and a universal law</note>, from which they established their ***Art***. Then, at last, if new ***Particulars*** and ***Examples*** were raised and brought forward which contradicted their decrees, they either subtly brought them back into order through distinctions or explanations of their rules, or else removed them crudely by making exceptions. As for the causes of ***Particular things*** that did not contradict them, they laboriously and stubbornly forced them to fit those ***Principles*** of theirs. Truly, that ***Natural History*** and ***Experience*** was not what it ought to have been (it was certainly far from it); and that "flying off" to the most ***General things*** <note>original: "Generalissima"; universal axioms or laws</note> ruined everything.

**CXXVI.**

It will also occur to some that we—because of a certain prohibition against making pronouncements and establishing certain principles until one has properly reached the most ***General things*** through intermediate steps—maintain a certain ***Suspension of judgment*** <note>original: "Suspensionem quandam judicii"; a practice of the Ancient Skeptics to avoid error by refusing to claim certainty.</note> and bring the matter toward ***Acatalepsia*** <note>original: "Acatalepsiam"; a Greek term meaning the belief that things are fundamentally "unknowable" or "un-graspable."</note>. We, however, do not contemplate or propose ***Acatalepsia***, but rather ***Eucatalepsia*** <note>original: "Eucatalepsiam"; a term Bacon coins meaning "good" or "sound" comprehension. He argues that truth is attainable if the right method is used.</note>. For we do not disparage the ***Senses***, but [assist]... <note>The text cuts off mid-word "ministramus," meaning "to serve" or "to assist."</note>

<summary>Bacon critiques the Ancient philosophers for jumping too quickly from specific facts to universal laws, then ignoring or "explaining away" any evidence that didn't fit. He distinguishes his own method of delaying judgment from Skepticism, arguing his goal is sound comprehension rather than declaring the world unknowable.</summary>

### CXXVII.

Someone might doubt rather than object: whether we speak only of **Natural Philosophy** <note>The study of nature and the physical universe, what we would call "Science" today.</note>, or also of the remaining Sciences—Logic, Ethics, and Politics—to be perfected according to our way. ### CXXVIII.

But it should not even be permitted to doubt regarding us: whether we wish to destroy and demolish the **Philosophy** and **Arts** and **Sciences** <note>Bacon refers here to the traditional academic subjects taught in universities, heavily based on Aristotle.</note> which we use. For we do not in any way obstruct those methods which have prevailed from nourishing **Disputations**, or adorning **Discourses**, or being applied and proving effective for **Professorial** duties and the conveniences of **Civil life**; finally, that they be received by consensus among men like a kind of coinage. Therefore, we shall not attempt to prove it further with words. Meanwhile, we constantly and distinctly warn that by these methods which are currently in use, neither can great progress be made in the doctrines and contemplation of the Sciences, nor can they be brought to the magnitude of **Works**.

# OF VERULAM

...[had we] ourselves fully and clearly completed the work, and did not constantly call others to share and join in our labors; we would have even abstained from words of this kind, lest they be taken as a proclamation of our own merit. But since the industry of others must be sharpened, and their minds excited and set on fire; it is fitting that we bring certain things back to men's minds.

First, therefore, the introduction of noble <term>Inventions</term> <note>original: "Inventorum"</note> seems to hold by far the foremost place among human actions: a judgment made by the ages of antiquity. For they <note>The ancient Greeks and Romans</note> bestowed divine honors upon the <term>Inventors of things</term>; but to those who served well in <term>Civil Affairs</term> (such as the Founders of cities and empires, Legislators, Deliverers of their homelands from long-standing evils, Overthrowers of Tyrannies, and those like them) they decreed only the honors of Heroes. And certainly, if one compares these correctly, he will find this judgment of the ancient age to be just. For the benefits of Inventions can extend to the whole human race; Civil benefits only to specific settlements of men. The latter also do not last beyond a few generations; the former, for almost all time. Furthermore, the <term>improvement of the State</term> in Civil matters usually proceeds not without force and disturbance: but Inventions bless, and confer a benefit without injury or sorrow to anyone.

Also, Inventions are like new Creations, and imitations of divine Works, as that poet <note>Likely referring to Virgil in the Aeneid, who praised those who "improved life through discovered arts."</note> sang so well:

Furthermore, it would not be out of place to distinguish three kinds and, as it were, degrees of human Ambition. The first is of those who desire to enlarge their own power in their native Country; which kind is common and base. The second is of those who strive to enlarge the power and empire of their Country among the human race: this certainly has more dignity, though no less greed. But if anyone should strive to restore and enlarge the power and empire of the human race itself over the Universe of things, that Ambition (if it may be so called) is without doubt both more sound and more majestic than the rest. To generate and superinduce a new Nature, or new Natures, upon a given Body, is the work and aim of human **Power**. But to find the **Form** <term>Form: In Bacon's philosophy, the "Form" is the objective internal law or structure that makes a thing what it is (e.g., the "Form" of heat is the specific motion that creates the sensation of heat).</term> of a given Nature, or its true difference, or its **Nurturing Nature** <note>original: "Naturam naturantem" — a Scholastic term referring to nature as an active, creative force or essence, rather than just the physical objects we see ("natura naturata").</note>, or the source of its emanation (for these are the terms we have that come closest to describing the thing), is the work and aim of human **Science**. And to these primary works are subordinated two other secondary works of a lower rank: To the former, the transformation of concrete Bodies from one thing into another, within the bounds of the *possible*; To the latter, the discovery, in every generation and motion, of the *latent process continued from the manifest efficient cause and manifest matter, up to the induced Form*; and similarly the discovery of the *latent configura-* <note>The word is completed on the next page as "configuration" or "schematism" (schematismi).</note>

II. How unhappily situated is the human **Science** currently in use, is clear even from those things commonly asserted. It is rightly laid down that: *To know truly, is to know through Causes.* <note>original: "Vere scire, esse per Causas scire." This is a foundational principle of Aristotelian philosophy which Bacon accepts, though he redefines what those causes are.</note> It is also not bad to establish four **Causes**: **Matter**, **Form**, **Efficient**, and **Final**. <term>Four Causes: Traditional Aristotelian categories: Matter (what it’s made of), Form (its essence/design), Efficient (what triggers the change), and Final (its purpose).</term> But of these, the **Final Cause** is so far from being useful that it actually corrupts the Sciences, except in the actions of Men. The discovery of **Form** is held to be a hopeless endeavor. As for the **Efficient** and the **Matter** (as they are usually sought and accepted—that is, as remote causes, without the latent process leading to the form), they are perfunctory and superficial things, contributing almost nothing to true and active Science. Nor, however, have we forgotten that we previously noted and corrected the error of the human mind in assigning the primary place of Essence to **Forms**. For although in Nature nothing truly exists except individual **Bodies**, performing pure individual acts according to law; yet in teaching, that very law—and its investigation, discovery, and explanation—is the foundation both for knowing and for operating. It is this law, and its constituent parts, that we understand by the name of **Forms**; especially since this word has become established and is in common use.

### IV.

Although the paths to human **Power** and **Science** are closely joined and almost the same, yet because of the harmful and deep-rooted habit of dwelling on abstractions, it is much safer to begin and raise the Sciences from those foundations which relate to the **Active part**, so that the **Active part** itself may mark and define the **Contemplative part**. <note>The "Active part" refers to practical application, while the "Contemplative" refers to theoretical knowledge. Bacon argues that practice should guide theory.</note> We must therefore see, in order to generate and introduce a certain **Nature** <term>Nature: Here used to mean a specific quality or property, such as "whiteness" or "heat."</term> upon a given **Body**, what kind of instruction, or what kind of direction or deduction, one would most desire; and this in simple and least obscure language.

Secondly, he will wish for something to be prescribed to him which does not bind or restrict him to certain specific means and particular modes of operating. For perhaps he might be destitute of such means, and lack the power and convenience of providing and procuring them. For example, we must inquire into what the **spirit** <term>Spiritus: In 17th-century science, "spirits" were highly refined, invisible fluids within matter that were thought to drive growth, movement, and decay.</term> is in every body, and what the **tangible essence** is. And likewise, we must study the **tangible essence** (which admits of no fewer variations than the spirit) and its filaments, fibers, and every kind of texture. Furthermore, the arrangement of the spirit throughout the bodily mass—its pores, passages, veins, and cells, and the first hints or attempts of the **organic body**—fall under the same inquiry. But even in these things, and indeed in every discovery of a **Latent Configuration**, a true and clear light is shed by **primary axioms** <term>Axiomatibus: Fundamental laws or principles derived from induction.</term>, which certainly dispel all darkness and difficulty.

**VIII.** Nor for this reason will the matter be reduced to the **Atom** <term>Atomum: An indivisible particle. Bacon critiques the ancient theory that the universe is made of hard, unchanging spheres moving in empty space.</term>, which presupposes a **Void** <term>Vacuum: A region of space containing no matter.</term> and **matter that is fixed** (both of which are false); rather, it will be reduced to **true particles**, as they are actually found to be. Nor, again, is there any reason for anyone to dread this subtlety as if it were impossible to explain; on the contrary, the more the **Inquiry** <note>original: *Inquisitio*</note> turns toward **Simple Natures** <note>The fundamental qualities or "alphabet" of the universe, such as heat, light, or density.</note>, the more everything will be clear and plain. The task is moved from the complex to the simple; from the immeasurable to the measurable; from the irrational to the calculable; and from the infinite and vague to the definite and certain—just as it is with the letters of the alphabet or the notes of musical harmony. Indeed, **Natural Inquiry** <note>The study of the physical world.</note> proceeds best when **Physics** <note>original: *Physicum*</note> ends in **Mathematics**. Again, let no one fear the vast numbers or the tiny fractions of things. For in matters that are handled by numbers, it is just as easy to set down or think of a thousand as it is to think of one; or a thousandth part of one as it is to think of a whole unit.

Therefore, the direct rays of the Sun seem to have little power, even on flat ground; nor do reflected rays, unless they are multiplied and united. This occurs when the Sun moves closer to the **perpendicular** <note>directly overhead, at a 90-degree angle to the earth</note>; for then the incidence of the rays creates more acute angles, so that the lines of the rays are closer together. Conversely, at great obliquities of the Sun <note>when the sun is at a low angle near the horizon</note>, the angles are very obtuse, and consequently the lines of rays are further apart. But in the meantime, it should be noted that there can be many operations of the Sun’s rays—and even belonging to the nature of **Heat** <note>original: "Calidi"</note>—which are not proportional to our sense of **touch** <note>original: "tactum nostrum"</note>; so that, in respect to us, they do not work to the point of warming, yet in respect to certain other bodies, they perform the work of Heat.

### *To the ninth, the fourteenth.* <note>This pairs with his ninth Affirmative Instance regarding boiling or heated liquids.</note>

To **boiling liquids** is subjoined the **Negative Instance** of the liquid's own nature. For no tangible liquid is found that is hot by its own nature and remains constantly warm; instead, **Heat** is only induced for a time as an **acquired nature** <note>original: "Natura ascititia"; heat that is not essential to the substance but added to it</note>. This is so much the case that things which are most "hot" in their power and operation—such as **spirit of wine** <note>original: "spiritus Vini"; concentrated alcohol</note>, chemical **oils of spices**, and even **oils of vitriol and sulfur** <note>original: "olea vitrioli & sulphuris"; what we now call concentrated sulfuric acid</note>, and the like, which burn after a short while—are cold to the initial touch. Moreover, the water of **natural baths**, when caught in a vessel and separated from its springs, **cools down** <note>original: "defervescit"</note> just like water heated by fire. It is true, however, that oily bodies are slightly less cold to the touch than watery ones; for instance, **Oil** is less cold than **Water**, and **Silk** is less cold than **Linen**. But this properly belongs to the **Table of Degrees of Cold**.

Many actions are common to both **Heat** and **Cold**, though for very different reasons. For snow, after a short while, seems to burn the hands of children; and cold protects meat from putrefaction <note>original: "putrefactione"; rotting or decay.</note> no less than fire does; and **Heat** contracts bodies into less space, which **Cold** things also do. However, it is more fitting to refer these and similar cases to the *Inquiry into Cold*.

### Aphorism XIII.

Thirdly, a **Presentation to the Intellect** <note>original: "Comparentia ad Intellectum"; a formal arrangement of data for the mind to process.</note> must be made of **Instances** in which the **Nature** under inquiry is present according to **more** and **less**; whether by comparing increase and decrease in the same subject, or by comparing different subjects to one another. For since the **Form** <term>Form|In Bacon's philosophy, the "Form" is the internal law or essence that makes a thing what it is (e.g., the underlying physical motion that creates the sensation of heat).</term> of a thing is the very **Thing** itself, and the **Thing** does not differ from its **Form** otherwise than the **Apparent** differs from the **Existing**, or the **External** from the **Internal**, or in relation to **Man** and in relation to the **Universe**; it follows absolutely that no **Nature** should be accepted as the true **Form** unless it always decreases when that **Nature** itself decreases, and similarly always increases when that **Nature** itself increases. We are, therefore, accustomed to call this Table the **Table of Degrees**, or the **Comparative Table**.

### Table of Degrees, or Comparative Instances
### in Heat.

First, therefore, we shall speak of those things which possess no degree of **Heat** whatsoever to the touch, but seem to have only a certain <term>Potential Heat|Heat that is not active or sensible to the touch, but exists as a latent capacity or a chemical readiness to ignite or warm up.</term>, or a disposition and preparation for becoming hot. After that, we shall finally descend to those things which are actually hot, or hot to the touch, and their strengths and **Degrees**.

1. Among solid and tangible bodies, nothing is found that is originally hot in its own **Nature**. For no stone, no metal, no sulfur, no mineral <note>original: "fossile"; in Bacon's time, this referred to anything dug out of the earth, not just organic remains.</note>, no wood, no water, nor the carcass of an animal is found to be hot. The hot waters in **Baths** <note>original: "Balneis"; referring to natural thermal springs.</note>, however, seem to be heated by accident—either by a flame or subterranean fire, such as is vomited from **Etna** and many other mountains; or from the **conflict of bodies** <note>original: "conflictu corporum"; Bacon's term for chemical reactions, specifically exothermic ones.</note>, just as **Heat** is produced in the dissolutions of iron and tin. Therefore, the degree of **Heat** in **Inanimate** things, as far as human touch is concerned, is nothing; nevertheless, those things differ in their **Degree of Cold**; for wood is not as cold as metal. But this pertains to the *Table of Degrees in Cold*.

2. Yet as for potential **Heats** and preparations for flame, many things are found <insert>to exist</insert>...

# VERULAMII

...most <note>Continuing the sentence from the previous page regarding the heat of the Sun.</note> intense, even in the hottest seasons of the year and times of day, it does not reach that degree of **Heat** which might set fire to or scorch the driest wood, straw, or even burnt linen, unless it is strengthened by burning glasses <note>original: "specula comburentia"; magnifying lenses or mirrors used to focus sunlight.</note>; however, it is able to draw out vapor from moist things.

15. According to the tradition of astronomers, some stars are categorized as more hot, and others as less hot. For among the planets, after the **Sun**, **Mars** is considered the hottest; then **Jupiter**, then **Venus**. On the other hand, the **Moon** is categorized as cold, and after that, **Saturn** is considered the coldest of all. Among the fixed stars, **Sirius** <note>The Dog Star.</note> is considered the hottest; then the **Heart of the Lion** <note>original: "Cor Leonis"; known today as the star **Regulus**.</note>, or **Regulus**, then the **Lesser Dog Star** <note>original: "Canicula"; usually referring to the star Procyon.</note>, etc.

16. The **Sun** heats more effectively the closer it approaches a perpendicular position, or the <term>Zenith|the point in the sky directly above an observer.</term>; this must also be believed regarding the other planets, according to their own measure of **Heat**. For example, **Jupiter** heats more in our region when it is positioned under the signs of **Cancer** or **Leo** than under **Capricorn** or **Aquarius**.

17. It is to be believed that the **Sun** itself, and the remaining planets, heat more in their <term>Perigees|original: "Perigæis"; the point in an orbit where a celestial body is closest to the Earth.</term>, due to their proximity to the earth, than in their <term>Apogees|original: "Apogæis"; the point in an orbit where a celestial body is furthest from the Earth.</term>. If it should happen that in a certain region the **Sun** is simultaneously in perigee and closer to a perpendicular position, it must necessarily heat more than in a region where the **Sun** is likewise in perigee but at a more oblique angle. Thus, a comparison of the elevation of the planets should be noted, according to how much it partakes of a perpendicular or oblique angle, depending on the variety of the regions.

24. In **Ignited** bodies, there are also different degrees of **Heat**, about which no diligent inquiry has yet been made. We consider the weakest heat to be from burnt linen; which we usually use to start a flame <note>Bacon refers to "tinder" used with flint and steel.</note>; and similarly from that spongy wood <note>original: "ligno illo spongioso"; likely touchwood or punky wood used to hold a spark.</note>, or dried cords, which are used for igniting **Cannons** <note>original: "tormentorum"; referring to the slow-matches used for early artillery.</note>. However, we judge the most vehemently hot of ignited bodies to be ignited metals, such as **Iron**, and **Copper**, and the rest. But further inquiry must be made regarding these.

25. Some **Ignited** bodies are found to be far **Hotter** than some flames. For ignited **Iron** is much hotter and more burning than the flame of **spirit of wine** <note>original: "spiritus vini"; an early term for concentrated alcohol or ethanol.</note>.

26. 39. After Air, we consider those bodies to be most sensitive to **Heat** which have been recently changed and compressed by **cold**, such as **Snow** and **Ice**; for these begin to dissolve and melt <note>original: "colliquari"; to turn liquid.</note> at any mild temperature. Those, however, once they have taken in **Heat**, retain it for a very long time; so much so that a brick, or stone, or glowing **iron**, placed and submerged in a basin of cold water, retains its **Heat** for about a quarter of an hour (more or less), so that it cannot be touched.

40. The smaller the mass of a body, the faster it heats up when a hot body is brought near it; this demonstrates that all **Heat** in our environment is in some way opposed to tangible matter <note>Bacon believed heat was a motion that acted against the "density" or "stubbornness" of solid matter, trying to expand or dissolve it.</note>.

41. **Heat**, as far as it relates to human sense and touch, is a variable and relative thing; so much so that lukewarm water, if the hand is gripped by **cold**, is felt to be hot; but if the hand is already warm, it feels cold.

### Aphorism XV.

And the work and duty of these three Tables we have been accustomed to call the *Presentation of Instances to the Intellect* <note>original: "Comparentiam Instantiarum ad intellectum"; this refers to the organized display of gathered data (The Tables of Presence, Absence, and Degree) so the mind can process them.</note>. Once the *Presentation* is made, *Induction* itself must be put to work. For there must be found—based on the *Presentation* of all and singular Instances—a Nature of such a kind that it is perpetually present when the given nature <note>The specific phenomenon being studied, such as heat.</note> is present, absent when it is absent, and increases or decreases with it, and is (as was said above) a limitation of a more common Nature. 

If the mind attempts to do this affirmatively from the very beginning (as it is always accustomed to do when left to itself), there will arise phantoms <note>original: "phantasmata"; Bacon uses this to describe the false images or "Idols" that the mind creates when it jumps to conclusions without a proper method.</note>, and mere opinions, and poorly defined notions, and axioms that must be corrected daily; unless one prefers (after the fashion of the Schools <note>Refers to the Scholastic philosophers of the Middle Ages, whom Bacon criticized for valuing debate over physical evidence.</note>) to fight for falsehoods. These will, without doubt, be better or worse according to the faculty and strength of the intellect at work. But it belongs entirely to God (the Giver and Creator of Forms) or perhaps to Angels and higher Intelligences, to know Forms through *Affirmation* immediately, and from the very start of contemplation. But it is certainly beyond the power of man; to whom it is granted only to proceed first through *Negatives* <note>The method of exclusion: ruling out what a thing is *not* until only the truth remains.</note>, and in the final place to end in *Affirmatives*, after every kind of exclusion.

### XVII.

We must be cautious, however, and a constant warning must be given, so that—since we seem to attribute such great importance to Forms—the things we say are not dragged toward those "Forms" to which men’s contemplations and thoughts have been accustomed until now.

### Example of the Exclusion, or Rejection
### of Natures from the Form of Heat.

1. By the rays of the Sun, Reject the **Elementary Nature**. <note>original: *Naturam Elementarem*. In Bacon's time, "elements" referred to the four traditional qualities of Earth, Water, Air, and Fire. Since the Sun provides heat from the heavens, heat is not restricted to the "element" of fire as found on Earth.</note>

2. By common Fire, and especially by subterranean Fires (which are most remote and mostly cut off from the Celestial rays), Reject the **Celestial Nature**. <note>original: *Naturam Cœlestem*. This shows that heat does not exclusively come from the stars or the heavens, as it can be found deep underground.</note>

3. By the heating of all kinds of bodies (that is, Minerals, Vegetables, the outer parts of Animals, Water, Oil, Air, and the rest) through proximity alone to Fire or another hot Body; Reject all **Variety**, or the **subtler Texture of bodies**. <note>Because heat can exist in any type of material, the specific internal structure or "texture" of a specific substance cannot be the essential cause of heat.</note>

4. By ignited Iron and Metals, which heat other bodies but are not at all diminished in weight or substance; Reject the **infusion** or **mixture of another hot substance**. <note>original: *inditionem sive mixturam substantiæ alterius*. Bacon is arguing that heat is not a physical "fluid" or substance that moves from one object to another, because the metal doesn't lose weight when it cools.</note>

5. By boiling Water and Air, and also by Metals and other Solids that are heated but not to the point of ignition or redness; Reject **Light** and **Brightness**. <note>original: *Lucem & Lumen*. This proves that something can be hot without glowing or emitting light.</note>

6. By the rays of the Moon and other Stars (except the Sun); Reject also **Light** and **Brightness**. <note>Conversely, these provide light without detectable heat, proving light and heat are not the same thing.</note>

### XX.

Nevertheless, because **Truth** emerges more quickly from error than from confusion, we think it useful that the **Understanding** be permitted—after the three Tables of **First Presentation** (such as we have laid out) have been completed and weighed—to set itself to work and attempt the task of the **Interpretation of Nature** in the affirmative; drawing both from the **Instances in the Tables** and from those which occur elsewhere. This kind of attempt we are accustomed to call the **Permission of the Understanding**, or the **Commencement of Interpretation**, or the **First Vintage**. <note>original: *Vindemiatio prima*. Bacon uses the metaphor of a "first harvest" or "first grape-gathering" to describe a preliminary hypothesis or result that is reached before the final proof is established.</note>

### *The First Vintage concerning the Form of Heat.*

It must be observed, however, that the **Form** of a thing is present (as is clearly evident from what has been said) in each and every **Instance** in which the thing itself is present; otherwise, it would not be the **Form**. <note>Recall that for Bacon, the "Form" is the essential law or nature of a quality, like the DNA of a physical property.</note> Therefore, no **contradictory instance** can possibly be given. Nevertheless, the **Form** is found to be far more conspicuous and evident in some **Instances** than in others; namely, in those where the **Nature of the Form** is less restrained, hindered, or limited by other **Natures**. These types of instances we are accustomed to call **Glances** <note>original: *Elucescentias*, meaning to shine forth or become visible.</note> or **Showy Instances**. <term>Showy Instances: Also known as "Ostensive Instances," these are examples where the specific quality under investigation (in this case, heat) stands out most clearly, unmasked by other distracting physical properties.</term>

Heat as perceived by the senses is a relative thing, pertaining to human experience rather than to the universe at large. Through the motion of friction, heat is produced without any pre-existing hot body; therefore, the "capacity to heat" is excluded from the **Form of Heat**. ### Aphorism XXI.

After the Tables of first Comparison <note>original: *Tabulas Comparentiæ*; these are the lists where Bacon organized instances where a nature (like heat) is present or absent.</note> and the Rejection or Exclusive Process, as well as the **First Vintage** <note>original: *Vindemiationem*; Bacon uses the metaphor of a "first harvest" to describe a preliminary hypothesis made before the investigation is complete.</note> made according to them, we must proceed to the remaining aids of the Understanding concerning the **Interpretation of Nature** and true and perfect **Induction**. We shall speak, therefore, in the first place, of **Prerogative Instances** <term>original: *Prærogativis Inſtantiarum*; these are specific types of observations or examples that carry more weight than others in proving a point.</term>; second, of the **Supports for Induction**; third, of the **Rectification of Induction**; fourth, of the **Variation of the Investigation** according to the Nature of the Subject; fifth, of the **Prerogatives of Natures** regarding Investigation, or of what should be investigated first and what later; sixth, of the **Limits of Investigation**, or the Synopsis of all...

### XXII.

Among the **Prerogative Instances** <term>original: *Prærogativas Instantiarum*; observations or examples that are more "privileged" or powerful than others in revealing the truth.</term>, we shall first propose **Solitary Instances**. These are "Solitary" when they exhibit the Nature under investigation in subjects that have nothing in common with other subjects except for that Nature itself. Conversely, they are also solitary if they *do not* exhibit the Nature in subjects that are similar in every other respect to those that do exhibit it. It is clear that such instances remove ambiguity and accelerate and strengthen the **Exclusion** process <note>The method of ruling out false causes to find the true nature of a thing.</note>, so that a few of them are as valuable as many others.

For example, if we are investigating the **Nature of Color**, "Solitary Instances" include prisms and crystalline gems, which produce colors not only within themselves but also externally upon a wall <note>original: *exerius* (likely a typo for *exterius*).</note>. Likewise, dewdrops and the like are solitary instances. These have nothing in common with the "fixed" colors found in flowers, colored gems, metals, woods, and so on, except for the color itself. From this, we can easily conclude that Color is nothing other than a modification of the image of light as it is sent in and received: in the first group (prisms), this happens through the different angles of light hitting the surface; in the second group (flowers/metals), it happens through the various textures and **schematisms** <term>original: *Schematismos*; the internal structural arrangement of the tiny parts of a body.</term> of the object. ### XXIII.

Among the **Prerogative Instances**, we shall place in the second rank **Migratory Instances** <term>original: *Instantias migrantes*; observations of a quality as it is actively appearing or disappearing in a subject.</term>. These are instances in which the **Nature under Investigation** migrates toward generation <note>toward coming into existence</note> when it did not previously exist; or, conversely, migrates toward "corruption" <note>in the sense of fading or perishing</note> when it previously existed. 

Therefore, in either of these reversals <note>original: *Antistrophe*; a term from rhetoric or music meaning a turning back or response</note>, such instances are always double; or rather, they are a single instance caught in motion or transition, brought to its opposite stage. Such instances not only accelerate and strengthen the **Exclusion** process <note>the method of ruling out false causes</note>, but they also drive the **Affirmative** side—that is, the **Form** <term>original: *Formam*; the true definition or underlying law of a nature</term> itself—into a narrow compass. For it is necessary that the **Form** of a thing be something that is introduced through such a **Migration**, or conversely [withdrawn] through such a...

But a remedy is easily applied to this matter through an **Exclusion** <note>the logical process of elimination</note> lawfully performed.

It must therefore be asked what has happened to the glass or the water through that **Migration**.

To be sure, it easily occurs to the **Understanding** <note>the faculty of the mind that processes information</note>—if corrupted by these kinds of **Efficient Causes** <note>the external agents or triggers that bring a quality into being</note>—that air is always required for the Form of Whiteness, or that Whiteness is only generated through transparent bodies; these ideas are entirely false and have been refuted through many **Exclusions** <note>the process of ruling out characteristics that are not essential to a nature</note>. Again, **red-hot iron** and similar things are so far from showing the progress of expansion that, on the contrary, because the **spirit** <note>original: *spiritus*; the thin, active matter within a solid</note> is blunted and broken by the compact and thick parts (which tame and bridle the expansion), the expansion itself is not at all visible to the senses. But the **Weather-glass** clearly shows expansion in **Air**, both visible, and progressive, and lasting, and not merely fleeting.

XXV. Among the **Prerogatives of Instances**, we shall place in the fourth spot **Clandestine Instances**, which we are also accustomed to call **Instances of the Twilight**. [...to be placed in a certain] order) such as Animals, Herbs; also Words, Letters, Characters, Historical Persons, and so forth; although some of these are more fit and convenient, others less so. **Places** <note>original: *Loci*; referencing the "Method of Loci," where one imagines a physical building and places "items" to be remembered in specific rooms</note> of this kind remarkably assist the Memory, and exalt it far beyond its natural powers. This species might rightly be called the ***Cutting Off of the Infinite*** <note>original: *Abscissio Infiniti*</note>.

For when someone strives to remember or recall something to Mind, if they have no prior notion or perception of what they seek, they certainly seek and labor and scurry here and there, as if in an **Infinite** space. But if they have some certain prior notion, that **Infinite** is immediately cut off, and the wandering of the Memory becomes more localized <note>original: *in vicino*; "in the neighborhood" or "nearby"</note>. 

In those three instances mentioned above, the prior notion is clear and certain. In the First [Order], there must be something that fits with the Order; in the Second [Places], there must be an **Image** which has some relation or agreement with those certain Places; in the Third [Verses], there must be Words that fall into a Verse. And thus the **Infinite** is cut off. Other instances, however, will provide this second Species: namely, whatever brings an **Intellectual** concept down to strike the **Sense** (a method which also flourishes especially in **Artificial Memory**).

Other Instances provide this second Species: such as those things that make an impression on a **strong Emotion** <note>original: *Affectu forti*</note>—specifically by striking Fear, Wonder, Shame, or Delight—assist the Memory. Other Instances provide this third Species: things that are most deeply impressed upon a **pure Mind** <note>original: *Mente pura*</note>, which is less preoccupied by what comes before or after; such as things learned in childhood, or what we contemplate just before sleep, and even the very first time anything happens; these stick more firmly in the Memory. Other Instances provide this fourth Species: a multitude of **Circumstances**, or **"Handles"** <note>original: *Ansarum*; literally "handles," used here as a metaphor for mental hooks or associations</note>, assist the Memory; such as writing in separate, non-continuous parts, or Reading and Reciting in a loud voice. Finally, other Instances provide this fifth Species: things that are expected and which excite **attention** stick better than those that merely fly past. Therefore, if you read a certain writing twenty times over, you will not learn it by heart as easily as if you read it ten times while attempting to recite it from memory in the intervals, and whenever the Memory fails, looking back at the book. 

So it is that there are, as it were, Six Minor Forms of those things which assist the Memory; namely:
1. The **Cutting Off of the Infinite** <note>as explained on the previous page, narrowing the field of search</note>;
<margin>c</margin> 2. The **Reduction of the Intellectual to the Sensible** <note>turning abstract ideas into physical images or objects</note>; 
3. Impression upon a **strong Emotion**; 
4. Impression upon a **pure Mind**; 
5. A **Multitude of Handles**; 
6. **Anticipation** <note>original: *Praexpectatio*</note>.

XXVII. Among the Prerogatives of Instances, we shall place in the sixth position **Conformable Instances**, or **Proportioned Instances**; which we are also accustomed to call **Parallels**, or **Physical Likenesses**. These are the instances that show the Likenesses and Pairings of things, not in "Lesser Forms" (as the Constitutive Instances do), but plainly in concrete objects. Thus, they are like the first and lowest steps toward the unification of Nature. They do not establish any Axiom <note>an established principle or law of nature</note> immediately from the start; but they merely indicate and observe a certain Harmony <note>original: *Consensum*</note> between Bodies. Nevertheless, although they do not advance the discovery of Forms <note>the underlying essence or "blueprint" of a property</note> very much, they nonetheless reveal the structure of the parts of the Universe with great utility, and perform a kind of anatomy on its members. Consequently, they sometimes lead us by the hand toward sublime and noble Axioms, especially those pertaining to the configuration of the World.

->VERULAMII<-

...he will also observe deviations more easily. Conversely, he who knows the **Deviations** will more accurately describe the **Ways** [of Nature].

And in this they also differ from **Monodic Instances** <note>original: *Instantiis Monodicis*; unique examples that are the only ones of their kind, like the sun or a magnet</note>, in that they much more effectively guide **Practice and Operation** <note>original: *Praxin & Operativam*; the practical application of knowledge to produce results</note>. For generating entirely new **Species** would be extremely difficult; but varying known species, and thereby producing many **Rare** and **Unusual** things, is less difficult. There is an easy transition from the **Miracles of Nature** to the **Miracles of Art**. For if Nature is caught even once in its variation, and the reason for it becomes clear, it will be easy to lead Nature by **Art** <note>meaning human skill, craft, or technology</note> to that same point where it strayed by **Chance**. And not only to that point, but elsewhere; since **Errors** in one direction show and open the way to errors and **Deflections** on all sides. Here, indeed, there is no need for examples, because of their great abundance. For a collection or a particular **Natural History** <note>original: *Historia Naturalis*; in Bacon's time, this referred to a systematic encyclopedia of facts and observations about the natural world</note> must be compiled of all **Monsters** and prodigious births of Nature; in short, of every **Novelty**, **Rarity**, and **Unusual** thing in Nature. This must be done, however, with the strictest selection, so that its credibility is certain. Those things must be held as especially suspect which depend in any way on religion, such as the **Prodigies of Livy** <note>original: *Prodigia Livii*; Titus Livius was a Roman historian who recorded many supernatural omens, such as raining blood or stones</note>. No less suspect are those things found in the writers of **Natural Magic** or even of **Alchemy**, and such men; who are, as it were, the suitors and lovers of fables. Instead, these things must be drawn from serious and trustworthy **History**, and from reliable reports.

...we call the ninth type **Boundary Instances** <note>original: *Instantias Limitaneas*</note>; which we are also accustomed to call **Participles** <note>original: *Participia*; in grammar, a participle shares the nature of both a verb and an adjective; Bacon uses it here for things that "share" the nature of two different species</note>. These are indeed those which exhibit species of Bodies that seem to be composed of two species, or **Rudiments** <note>the beginnings or undeveloped forms</note> between one species and another. These instances may rightly be numbered among **Monodic** <note>unique</note> or **Heteroclite** <note>irregular</note> instances. For they are Rare and Extraordinary in the universe of things. Nevertheless, because of their dignity, they must be treated and placed separately. For they are excellent at indicating the composition and fabric of things, and they suggest the causes for the Number and Quality of the Ordinary Species in the Universe, and they lead the Intellect from what is, toward what can be.

Examples of these are: Moss, between Decay and a Plant; certain Comets, between Stars and fiery Meteors; flying fish, between **Birds** and **Fish**; **Bats**, between **Birds** and **Four-legged animals**: Also

> The monkey, that most hideous beast, how similar it is to us; <note>original Latin: *Simia quam similis turpissima bestia nobis*; a quote from the Roman poet Ennius</note>

and the biformed offspring of animals, mixed from different species; and similar things.

On the contrary, this must be held as certain: the ways and methods of producing things and **Works** <note>original: *Opera*; the practical outputs of human skill</note> that have been discovered and noted so far are mostly poor little things; all greater power depends on and is derived in an orderly way from the sources of **Forms** <note>the fundamental laws or essential natures of things</note>, none of which have yet been discovered.

Therefore (as we have said elsewhere), if someone had thought about **Machines** and **Battering Rams** <note>original: *Arietes*</note> such as existed among the Ancients—even if they had done so persistently and spent a lifetime on it—they would never have stumbled upon the invention of **Firearms** operating by **Gunpowder** <note>original: *Pulverem pyrium*</note>. However, nothing represents or anticipates Chance (which usually operates only over long centuries) except for the discovery of **Forms**.

Now, there is no need to bring forward particular examples of this kind of instances, because of their abundance. ### XXXII.
From what has been said before, it is clear that those five kinds of instances of which we have spoken—namely, **Conformable Instances**, **Monodic Instances**, **Deviating Instances**, **Limiting Instances**, and **Instances of Power**—should not be reserved until a specific Nature is being investigated. The remaining instances, which we proposed in the first place, as well as many of those which will follow, must indeed be reserved for specific investigations. 

However, a collection of these five should be made immediately from the start, as a kind of **particular history**. This is because they digest the things that enter the Intellect and correct its depraved complexion. For the Intellect must necessarily be imbued, infected, and finally perverted and distorted by the daily and common occurrences of life.

Therefore, these instances are to be applied as a kind of preparation to rectify and purge the Intellect. For whatever draws the Intellect away from the customary levels and smooths its surface for receiving the **dry light** <term>Lumen siccum: a term from Heraclitus, used by Bacon to describe a clear, objective intellect unclouded by the "moisture" of human passions or personal biases</term> and the purity of true notions.

Moreover, instances of this kind pave and prepare the way for the **Operative** <note>original: *Operativam*; the practical application of science to produce "works" or inventions</note>; as we shall say in its proper place, when we speak of **Deductions to Practice** <note>original: *Deductionibus ad Praxin*</note>.

### NOVUM ORGANUM. 221

In the eleventh place, we name **Instances of Companionship**, and also **Hostile Instances**; which we have also been accustomed to call **Instances of Fixed Propositions**. These are instances which exhibit some Body or Concrete substance in which the **Nature under Investigation** <note>original: *Natura Inquisita*; the specific quality or phenomenon the scientist is currently trying to define, such as heat or light</note> perpetually follows as if it were an inseparable companion; or conversely, in which the Nature under Investigation perpetually flees and is excluded from the company, like a foe and an enemy. 

For from instances of this kind, certain and universal propositions are formed, whether **Affirmative** or **Negative**; in these, the Subject will be such a Body in the Concrete, and the Predicate will be the Nature under Investigation itself. 

For indeed, particular propositions are not at all **Fixed** where the Nature under Investigation is found in some Concrete substance to be fluid and changeable—that is, arriving (or acquired) or, on the other hand, departing (or laid aside). 

Therefore, Particular Propositions do not have any great **Prerogative** <note>In Bacon's system, a "Prerogative" instance is one that carries more weight or authority in proving a rule than common instances</note>, except only in the case of **Migration** <note>original: *Migrationis*; referring to instances where a nature is seen in the process of beginning or ending, such as white foam appearing on clear water</note>, of which we have spoken before. 

And nevertheless, even those Particular Propositions, when compared and collated with Universal ones, are very helpful, as will be discussed in its proper place. And yet, even in these Universal Propositions, we do not require an exact or absolute affirmation or denial. For it is sufficient for the purpose at hand even if they allow for some singular or rare exception.

The use of **Instances of Companionship**, however, is to narrow down the **Affirmative of the Form** <term>Affirmativam Formæ: the positive definition of the "Form" or the underlying law of nature that explains why a phenomenon exists</term>. For just as in **Migratory Instances** <note>original: *Instantiis Migrantibus*</note>, [the Form] is narrowed...

**Affirmative of the Form**; see that it must necessarily be posited that the Form of a thing is something which is instilled or destroyed through that **Act of Migration** <note>A process where a quality begins or ends in a substance, like heat entering a cooling metal</note>: So also in **Instances of Companionship**, the **Affirmative of the Form** is narrowed down; so that it must necessarily be posited that the Form of a thing is something which enters into such a concrete body, or conversely, shrinks from it; so that whoever well knows the Constitution or <term>Schematism</term> <note>original: *Schematismum*; the internal structural arrangement of the minute parts of a body</note> of such a body, will not be far from bringing to light the form of the **Nature under Investigation**.

For example: let the Nature under Investigation be **Heat**. An **Instance of Companionship** is Flame. For indeed, in water, air, stone, metal, and very many other things, Heat is mobile, and can arrive and depart: but all Flame is hot, so that Heat perpetually follows in the concrete substance of Flame. But no **Hostile Instance** of Heat is found among us <note>A substance that by its very nature can never be heated</note>. For nothing is certain to our senses concerning the depths of the Earth; but of those bodies known to us, there is absolutely no concrete substance that is not capable of receiving Heat.

But again, let the Nature under Investigation be **Consistency** <note>The quality of being solid or having a fixed shape, as opposed to being fluid</note>: the **Hostile Instance** is **Air**. For metal can flow and can be consistent; likewise glass; even water can be consistent when it is frozen: but it is impossible for Air ever to be consistent or to shed its fluidity.

### XXXV.
Among the **Prerogative Instances**, we place in the thirteenth spot **Instances of Alliance** or **Union**. These are those which mingle and unite Natures that are thought to be **Heterogeneous** <note>original: *Heterogeneæ*; consisting of different kinds or unrelated types</note>; and for such they are noted and marked by the accepted divisions of the day.

But **Instances of Alliance** show that operations and effects, which are assigned to one of those "Heterogeneous" groups as being unique to them, also belong to others of those groups. This proves that this **Heterogeneity** (which exists in common opinion) is not true or essential, but is nothing other than a **Modification of a common Nature**. Therefore, their use is excellent for raising and elevating the **Intellect** from **Differences** to **Genera** <note>original: *Genera*; general classes or broader categories</note>, and for removing the masks and phantoms of things, as they occur and come forth disguised in **Concrete substances**.

...and the **Heat of Fire**: and that these Heats (especially one of them, compared to the other two) are different in their very essence and species, or specific nature, and are clearly **heterogeneous** <note>original: *hæterogenei*; consisting of unrelated types. Bacon is critiquing the common view that celestial and terrestrial heat are different substances</note>. This was believed because the **Heat of the Heavens** and of **Animals** generates and nourishes, whereas the **Heat of Fire**, on the contrary, corrupts and destroys. Therefore, an **Instance of Alliance** is that well-known experiment where a vine branch is brought inside a house where a fire is kept constantly burning; as a result, the grapes ripen even a full month earlier than those outside. Thus, the ripening of fruit—even while still hanging on the plant—can be achieved by **Fire**, although this very task is seen as the specific work of the **Sun**. Because of this starting point, the **Intellect**, having rejected the idea of essential heterogeneity, easily rises to investigate what the actual **Differences** are between the Heat of the Sun and the Heat of Fire, which cause their operations to be so dissimilar even though they both share a common **Nature**.

These **Differences** are found to be four: namely, First, that the Heat of the Sun, compared to the Heat of Fire, is far gentler and milder in degree. Second, that it is (especially as it is carried to us through the **Air**) much more humid in quality. Third (which is the main point), that it is highly unequal—approaching and increasing, then receding and diminishing—a quality that contributes most to the **Generation** <term>Generation; the process of coming into being or biological growth</term> of bodies. For ***Aristotle*** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose theories of "Generation and Corruption" dominated science until Bacon's time</note> rightly asserted that the principal cause of the **Generations** and **Corruptions** <term>Corruption; the process of decay or breaking down</term> that take place here among us on the surface...

# VERULAMII

...of the Earth, is the oblique path of the Sun through the **Zodiac**. From this, the **Heat of the Sun**—partly through the alternations of **Day and Night**, and partly through the successions of **Summer and Winter**—becomes unequal in marvelous ways. Yet, that man <note>Bacon is referring to Aristotle, whom he frequently criticizes for being too theoretical and "authoritative" rather than observational.</note> does not cease to immediately corrupt and deprave what he had correctly discovered. For as the self-appointed **Arbiter of Nature** (as is his habit), he very authoritatively assigns the cause of **Generation** <term>Generation; the process of something coming into being, such as birth or growth</term> to the **Approach of the Sun** <note>original: *Accessui Solis*; the Sun's relative movement toward the earth in Spring/Summer.</note>; and the cause of **Corruption** <term>Corruption; the process of decay, death, or dissolution</term> to its **Recession** <note>original: *Recessui*; the Sun's movement away in Autumn/Winter.</note>.

In reality, both of these (the Approach and the Recession of the Sun) provide the cause for both Generation and Corruption, not respectively, but as it were indifferently. This is because the **inequality** of Heat serves the Generation and Corruption of things, while **equality** <note>Bacon means a constant, unchanging temperature.</note> serves only their **Conservation** <note>original: *Conservationi*; preservation or keeping something in its current state.</note>.

There is also a **Fourth Difference** between the Heat of the Sun and of Fire, which is of truly great importance: namely, that the Sun instills its operations through long spans of time, whereas the operations of Fire (driven by the impatience of men) are brought to a conclusion over much shorter intervals.

Among the **Prerogative Instances** <term>categories of evidence that hold special weight or authority in an investigation</term>, we will place in the fourteenth position *Instances of the Cross* <note>original: "Instantias Crucis"; these are the origin of the modern term "crucial experiment"</note>; taking the name from the crosses <note>signposts or guideposts</note> erected at crossroads, which indicate and signal the division of ways.
