Therefore, let the **Inquiry** now be reduced (if it pleases, and dismissing those two prior types of **Motion**) to this last one; and let it be inquired if any such **Raising** happens through **Sympathy** or a **Magnetic force**. And yet, first it is manifest that all the **Waters**, as they are placed in the **Trench** or **Hollow of the Sea**, cannot be lifted up all at once, because there would be nothing to succeed <note>fill the space</note> at the bottom; so much so that if there were in the **Waters** some desire of this kind to lift themselves up, that desire would nevertheless be broken and restrained by the **Connection of things** <note>original: "Nexu rerum"; the physical continuity of the universe</note>, or (as they commonly say) **lest a vacuum be created** <note>original: "ne detur Vacuum"; the traditional belief that nature prevents the existence of empty space</note>. It remains, therefore, that the **Waters** are raised in one part, and by this they are diminished and recede in another.

Truly, it must necessarily follow that since that **Magnetic force** <note>Bacon refers to a natural attraction, likely from the moon or heavens, which he calls "magnetic" by analogy</note> cannot act upon the **Whole** <note>the entire body of water at once</note>, it must act most intensely around the **Middle**; thus, it would lift the **Waters** in the **Middle**, while those same waters, once raised, would successively desert and abandon the sides.

This, indeed, is not difficult to test in straits using sounding lines <note>original: "lineas nauticas"; cords used by sailors to measure depth</note>; namely, whether during **Refluxes** toward the **Middle of the Sea**, the sea is deeper than it is during **Fluxes**. It should be noted, however, that if this is the case, it would mean (contrary to what is commonly believed) that the **Waters** are actually lifting themselves during **Refluxes**, and lowering themselves during **Fluxes**, so that they spread out to cover and flood the shores.

The Instance of the ***Cross*** <note>original: "Instantia Crucis"; a decisive observation that determines which of two paths or theories is correct</note> upon this subject will be as follows. If some ***Motion*** is found in the ***Ocean*** from ***East*** to ***West***, although it be very faint and weak; if the same ***Motion*** is found somewhat more rapid in the ***Air***, especially within the ***Tropics***, where because of the larger ***Circles*** <note>the greater circumference of the Earth at the equator</note> it is more perceptible; if the same ***Motion*** is found in the lower ***Comets***, now become lively and strong; if the same ***Motion*** is found in the ***Planets***, yet so distributed and graduated that the closer a body is to the ***Earth***, the slower it is, and the further away, the faster, and finally in the ***starry Heaven*** it is swiftest; then certainly ***Diurnal Motion*** <note>the daily rotation of the sky</note> must be accepted as real in the ***Heavens***, and the Motion of the ***Earth*** must be rejected. 

This is because it will be manifest that the ***Motion*** from ***East*** to ***West*** is plainly ***Cosmic***, and arising from the ***Consent of the Universe*** <note>original: "Consensu Universi"; the idea that the entire physical world acts in harmony or shares a collective impulse</note>, which, being most rapid at the ***Summits of Heaven***, gradually fails, and at last ceases and is extinguished in the ***Immobile***, namely the ***Earth***.

Likewise, let the ***Nature under Investigation*** be that other ***Motion of Rotation*** celebrated among ***Astronomers***, which is resisting and contrary to the ***diurnal Motion***—namely, the motion from ***West*** to ***East***. This is the motion which the ancient ***Astronomers*** attribute to the ***Planets***, and even to the ***starry Heaven***, but which ***Copernicus*** and his ***Followers*** attribute to the ***Earth*** as well. Let it be asked whether any such ***Motion*** is found in the ***nature*** of things, or whether it is rather a thing fabricated and supposed for the ***Shorthand*** and ***Conveniences of Calculation***, and for that beautiful idea—namely, of explaining ***Celestial Motions*** by...

And it is most certain, if we behave for a moment like common people—dismissing the inventions of **Astronomers** and the **Schools** <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional university scholars of Bacon's time who followed Aristotelian logic</note>, who habitually and unfairly do violence to the senses in many things and prefer the more obscure—that this **Motion** is exactly as it appears to the senses. But if nothing of this kind is found, it must be held as suspect, and...

...hold. The reasons for this latter opinion are based chiefly on this: that the Moon reflects the rays of the Sun; and it does not seem that the reflection of light occurs except from solid bodies.

We also see that **Dark Air** behind windows at night reflects the light of a candle no less than a **Dense Body** does. For it is manifest that this cannot [be attributed to the air...]

The **Schools** <note>Bacon refers to the Scholastic philosophers who dominated the universities of his time.</note> and common opinion, however, only deal with that former **Desire**. Meanwhile, they hardly notice that, even if this were true (assuming the **Flame** is actually generated), the generation of that **Flame** could nevertheless be hindered by a mass large enough to compress and suffocate it; so that the matter is not brought to that **Necessity** of which they speak. For they are correct in thinking that **Expansion** must occur, and that **Discharge** or the removal of the obstructing **Body** must follow, *if* the **Flame** is generated. But that **Necessity** is clearly avoided if that solid mass [suppresses] the **Flame**...

# NOVUM ORGANUM.

->247<-

...by **contrary Natures** <note>original: "contrariis Naturis"; completing the sentence from the previous page: "the flame by no means remains the same in number, but ceases because of the contrary natures surrounding it."</note> surrounding it, it suffers force and is destroyed.

Therefore, concerning this subject, there could be a **Crucial Instance** <term>Instantia Crucis</term> <note>Also known as an "Instance of the Fingerpost," this is a decisive experiment that points the way forward when a researcher is at a crossroads between two possible explanations.</note> such as this. We see, in larger **Fires**, how high the **Flames** ascend into the air. For the wider the **Base of the Flame** <term>Basis Flammæ</term>, the higher the **Summit** <term>Vertex</term>. Thus, it seems the process of **Extinction** begins around the **Sides** <term>Latera</term>, where the flame is compressed and distressed by the **Air**. But the **Inner Core of the Flame** <term>Meditullia Flammæ</term>, which the air does not touch but is surrounded on all sides by other flame, remains numerically the same entity; it is not extinguished until it is gradually narrowed by the **Air** surrounding it from the **Sides**. Thus, every flame is **Pyramidal**, being broader at the **Base** near the fuel <note>original: "fomitem"; the source of the fire, such as wood or oil.</note>, but sharper at the **Summit** where the air is hostile and no fuel is supplied. But **Smoke** is narrower at the **Base** and expands as it ascends, becoming like an **Inverted Pyramid**. Some other operations at a distance might also be added. Indeed, action of this kind occurs both in **Time**, through moments, not in an instant of time; and in **Space**, through degrees and distances. Therefore, there is some moment of time and some interval of space in which that power or action lingers in the medium between those two bodies that stir the motion. But that **Magnetic** or **Coitive Power** <term>Coitiva Virtus</term> <note>From the Latin 'coitus', meaning a coming together or joining; the force that draws two things toward one another.</note> treats the Medium as **indifferent** <note>original: "adiaphora"; a Greek term meaning things that make no difference or are neutral.</note>, nor is the Power hindered by any kind of Medium. But if that Power or Action has nothing to do with the intervening body, it follows that it is a **Natural Action** <term>Actio Naturalis</term> subsisting for some time and in some place without a Body, since it resides neither in the terminal bodies nor in the intervening ones. Therefore, Magnetic Action could be an **Instance of Divorce** <term>Instantia Divortii</term> regarding **Corporeal Nature** and **Natural Action**. 

To this, a corollary or "profit" may be added that should not be overlooked: namely, that a proof may be drawn even from the physical senses to show that there are **Separate and Incorporeal Substances** <term>Substantiæ separatæ</term> <note>In traditional philosophy, these are beings or entities (like souls or spirits) that exist independently of physical matter.</note>. For if a Natural Power and Action, emanating from a body, can subsist for some time and in some place entirely without a body, it is nearly certain that it could also, in its very origin, emanate from an Incorporeal Substance. For it seems that a physical body is no less required to sustain and carry a natural action than it is to excite or generate it.

### NEW ORGANON. 251

**XXXVIII.** There follow five Orders of **Instances**, which we have been accustomed to call by the single general name **Instances of the Lamp** <term>Instantiae Lampadis</term>, or of **Primary Information** <term>Informatio Prima</term>. These are the ones that assist the **Senses**. For since every **Interpretation of Nature** <term>Interpretatio Naturae</term> begins with the Senses, and from the perceptions of the Senses—by a straight, constant, and fortified path—leads to the perceptions of the **Intellect** <term>Intellectus</term> (which are true Notions and Axioms), it follows that the more abundant and exact the representations or provisions of the Sense itself are, the more easily and successfully everything will proceed.

Of these five **Instances of the Lamp**:
1. The **First** strengthen, enlarge, and rectify the immediate actions of the Senses.
2. The **Second** lead that which is **non-sensible** <note>Things too small, too distant, or too subtle to be perceived normally.</note> to that which is **Sensible**.
3. The **Third** indicate the continuous **Processes** or **Series** of those things and motions which (for the most part) are not noticed except in their final result or at specific intervals.
4. The **Fourth** substitute something for the Senses in cases of total **deprivation** <note>When a sense is completely unable to perceive something, such as seeing through an opaque wall.</note>.
5. The **Fifth** excite the attention and notice of the Senses, and at the same time limit the **subtlety of things** <note>This refers to narrowing down focus so the mind isn't overwhelmed by complex details.</note>.

We must now speak of each of these individually.

For nothing is truer in Nature than that twin proposition: *From nothing, nothing is made* <note>original: *Ex nihilo nihil fieri*</note>; nor, *Anything is reduced to nothing*; but that the **Quantity of Matter** itself, or the **total Sum**, remains constant, and is neither increased nor diminished.

   Nor is that [principle] less true: *That from that Quantity of Matter, within the same spaces or dimensions, more and less is contained, according to the diversity of bodies*; as in **Water** more is contained, in **Air** less: So much so that if anyone should assert that a certain volume of Water can be turned into an equal volume of Air, it would be the same as if he said that Something can be reduced to Nothing. Conversely, if anyone should assert that a certain volume of Air can be turned into an equal volume of Water, it would be the same as if he said that Something can be made from nothing. And from this abundance and Scarcity of Matter, those Notions of **Dense and Rare**, which are understood in various and confused ways, are properly derived.

   That third Assertion must also be assumed, which is also certain enough: that this "More and Less" of Matter in this or that body, of which we speak, can be reduced to **Calculations** (once a comparison has been made) and **Exact Proportions**, or those close to exact. As if someone were to say, that there is in a given volume of **Gold** such [a specific amount of matter...]

# VERULAMII <note>Referring to Francis Bacon’s title, Baron Verulam</note>

Similarly, in general, all refined **Tests** <note>original: *Probationes*</note> of bodies—whether **Natural** or **Artificial**—by which **True** things are distinguished from **Counterfeits**, and **Better** from **Baser**, must be referred to this category. For they bring the **Non-Sensible** <note>that which cannot be perceived by the senses</note> to the **Sensible**. They are, therefore, to be sought after from every side with diligent care.

As for the fifth kind of **Concealment** <note>original: *Latitantiæ*; the state of being hidden or "latent"</note>, it is manifest that the action of the **Sense** is performed in **Motion**, and **Motion** in **Time**. Therefore, if the **Motion** of any body is either so slow or so swift that it is not proportional to the **Moments** <note>the smallest measurable intervals of time</note> in which the action of the **Sense** is performed, the **Object** is not perceived at all. This is seen in the motion of the **Hand of a Clock** <note>original: *Indicis Horologii*</note>, and again in the motion of a **Musket Ball** <note>original: *Pilæ Sclopeti*</note>. Furthermore, **Motion** that is not perceived because of its slowness is easily and commonly brought to the **Sense** by the **Summation of Motion** <note>observing the total change after a period of time, such as seeing where a clock hand has moved after an hour</note>; but motion that is unperceived due to its velocity has not yet been well-measured. Nevertheless, the **Investigation of Nature** <term>Inquisitio Naturæ; Bacon's term for the systematic scientific study of the natural world</term> requires this to be done in some cases.

The sixth kind, however—where the **Sense** is hindered because of the "nobility" <note>the overwhelming power, intensity, or brilliance</note> of the **Object**—admits of a **Bringing-forth** <note>original: *Deductionem*; the process of making something perceptible to the human mind</note>. This is done either by the **Removal** <note>original: *Elongationem*; moving the object further away</note> of the **Object** further from the **Sense**; or by the **Dulling** <note>original: *Hebetationem*</note> of the **Object** through the **Interposition of a Medium** that weakens the object without annihilating it; or by the **Admittance and Reception** of a **Reflected Object** where the **Direct** impact is too strong, such as seeing the **Sun** in a **basin of water**.

# NEW ORGANON <note>original: *Novum Organum*</note>

...the **Sense** <note>This completes the word *sensus* from the previous page</note> is so overwhelmed by the **Object** that there is no room for a new impression; this occurs almost exclusively in the sense of **Smell** and **Odors**, and it does not contribute much to the matter at hand. Sometimes, however, the **Bringing-forth** is made not to the human **Sense**, but to the **Sense** of some other **Animal**, whose **Sense** excels the human one in certain respects: such as the perception of some **Odors** by a **Dog**; or of **Light**, which exists hidden in air that is not lit from the outside, by a **Cat**, an **Owl**, and similar **Animals** that see at night. For *Telesio* <note>Bernardino Telesio (1509–1588), an Italian natural philosopher whose work on the nature of heat and light influenced Bacon</note> rightly noted that there is even in the **Air** itself a certain original **Light**, albeit faint and thin, and for the most part not useful to the eyes of humans or most animals. He argued this because those **Animals** whose **Sense** is proportioned to this kind of light see at night; it is less believable that this happens either without any light at all or through some internal light.

And this must certainly be noted: we are dealing here with the **Deficiencies** <note>original: *Destitutionibus*; instances where the sense simply fails to perceive a thing</note> of the **Senses** and their remedies. For the **Fallacies of the Senses** <note>errors in judgment or illusions</note> should be referred to their own proper **Investigations** into **Sense and the Sensible**—except for that great **Fallacy of the Senses**, namely, that they establish the lines of things according to the **analogy of Man**, and not according to the **analogy of the Universe**. <note>This is a central theme in Bacon's philosophy: the tendency of humans to project their own nature, patterns, and expectations onto the natural world, rather than seeing nature as it truly is.</note> This cannot be corrected except by **Reason** and **universal Philosophy**.

### LORD VERULAM <note>original: *Verulamii*; referring to Francis Bacon, Baron Verulam</note>

**XLI.** Among the **Prerogative Instances** <note>original: *Prærogativas Instantiarum*; these are "privileged" or "special" examples that have more power than others to guide the mind toward the truth of nature</note> we shall place in the eighteenth position the **Instances of the Way**; which we have also been accustomed to call **Traveling Instances**, and **Articulated Instances**. These are the instances which indicate the motions of **Nature** as they are continued step-by-step. 

This class of **Instances** tends to escape **Observation** rather than the **Sense** itself. For the negligence of men regarding this matter is remarkable. They contemplate **Nature** only sporadically <note>original: *desultorie*; literally "like a trick-rider," jumping from one horse to another</note> and at intervals, and only after bodies have been completed and finished, rather than in their actual operation. 

But if anyone desired to explore and contemplate the ingenuity and industry of some **Artisan**, he would not only wish to see the raw materials of the **Art** and then the finished works; he would instead desire to be present while the **Artisan** works and advances his labor. A similar approach must be taken toward **Nature**. 

For example: if one is inquiring into the **growth of Plants**, he must inspect the process from the very sowing of a seed. This can easily be done by pulling up seeds—almost every day—that have remained in the earth for two, three, or four days, and so on, and looking at them with diligent attention. One must observe how and when the seed begins to swell and grow turgid, and as if filled with **spirit** <note>original: *spiritu*; in Bacon’s physics, "spirit" refers to the invisible, active, and thin matter within all things that drives change and motion</note>; then how it breaks its small skin and emits fibers, with a certain lifting of itself upwards in the meantime, unless the earth is too stubborn; and how it also sends out fibers, partly as roots downwards, and partly as stems

# VERULAM 288

### XLII. Among the **Prerogative Instances** <term>Prærogativas Instantiarum<gloss>Specifically chosen examples or "privileged" observations that carry more weight than others in proving a scientific rule</gloss></term>, we shall place in the nineteenth spot **Instances of Supplement** <note>original: *Instantias Supplementi*</note>, or of **Substitution**; which we have also been accustomed to call **Instances of Refuge** <note>original: *Instantias Perfugii*</note>. These are those which supply information where the **Senses** are entirely destitute; and therefore we flee to them when specific instances cannot be obtained. Substitution occurs in two ways: either through **Graduation** <note>original: *Graduationem*; meaning comparing different degrees of the same quality</note>, or through **Analogy**.

For example: no medium can be found that completely blocks the operation of a **Magnet** <note>original: *Magnetis*</note> in moving iron—not interposed Gold, nor Silver, nor Stone, nor Glass, Wood, Water, Oil, Cloth or fibrous bodies, Air, Flame, or the like. Yet, through an exact trial, perhaps some medium could be found that would inhibit its power more than another, comparatively and in some degree. For instance, perhaps a magnet does not pull iron through a certain thickness of gold as well as it does through an equal space of air, or through a certain amount of heated silver as well as through cold; and so on with similar things. For we have not performed the **Experiment** <note>original: *Experimentum*</note> on these ourselves; but it is sufficient, however, for them to be proposed as an example. 

Similarly, no body is found here among us that does not receive **Heat** when brought near a fire. Yet **Air** receives heat far more quickly than **Stone**. And such is the Substitution that is made through **Degrees**.

Substitution through **Analogy**, however, is certainly useful, but less certain; and therefore it should be used with judgment...

->## NOVUM ORGANUM.<-

...applied in a certain way. This occurs when the **Non-sensible** <note>original: *Non-sensibile*; things that cannot be directly perceived by the human senses</note> is brought down to the **Senses**; not through the sensible actions of the invisible body itself, but through the observation of some related sensible body. 

For example: if we are investigating the **Mixture of Spirits** <term>Mistura Spirituum<gloss>In Bacon's natural philosophy, "spirits" are not ghosts, but extremely thin, invisible, and active "fluids" or gases that exist within all matter, especially living things</gloss></term>, which are invisible bodies; there seems to be a certain kinship between bodies and their **fuels** <note>original: *fomites*</note> or nourishments. Now, the fuel of **Flame** appears to be **Oil** and **Fatty substances** <note>original: *Pinguja*</note>; while the "fuel" of **Air** is **Water** and **Watery substances**. For flames multiply themselves upon the vapors of oil, and air multiplies itself upon the vapors of water. 

Therefore, we should look at the mixture of Water and Oil, which reveals itself to our Senses; since the mixture of Air and the nature of Flame escapes the Senses. Now, Oil and Water mix very imperfectly through simple blending or shaking; however, they are mixed accurately and delicately in herbs, in blood, and in the parts of animals. Thus, something similar might happen regarding the mixture of the flaming and airy natures in "spiritual" <note>meaning gaseous or vaporous</note> substances. While they do not blend well through simple mixing, they seem to be mixed within the **spirits of plants and animals**; especially since every **Animate Spirit** <term>Spiritus Animatus<gloss>The life-force or vital heat believed to animate living organisms, sustained by a balance of oily and watery nutrients</gloss></term> feeds upon both types of moisture, the watery and the fatty, as its fuels.

For example, while one action of a *different* kind does not disturb or hinder another (as we just described), yet within the *same* kind, one action often overpowers and extinguishes another. Examples include: the light of the **Sun** over the light of a **Glow-worm**; the sound of a **Cannon** <note>original: *Bombardæ*; literally a bombard or early artillery piece</note> over the human voice; a stronger **Odor** over a more delicate one; more intense **Heat** over a milder one; or a **Sheet of Iron** <margin>c</margin> placed between a **Magnet** and another piece of **Iron**, which stops the magnet’s operation. Afterward, we calculated how much the space had been diminished by that Compression; and we understood that the Water had undergone that much Compression (though only when subdued by **great force**).

However, **more Solid**, **Dry**, or more **Compact** bodies—such as **Stones** and **Wood**, as well as **Metals**—tolerate even less **Compression** or **Extension**, which in them is almost imperceptible. Instead, they release themselves from pressure either by **Breaking**, or by **Moving forward**, or by other attempts at escape, as seen in the **Bending** of Wood or Metal, or in the movements of **Clocks** <note>original: *Horologiis moventibus*; likely referring to the tension and release of springs in mechanical timepieces</note>...

...appears through the folding of a metal plate, in the flight of projectiles, by hammering, and through countless other motions. ### XLVI.
Among the **Prerogative Instances** <term>Prærogativas Instantiarum: "Privileged examples" or "Special Cases" that Bacon identifies as being particularly useful for understanding the laws of nature.</term>, we shall place in the twenty-second position the **Instances of the Course**, which we are also accustomed to call **Instances of the Water-clock** <term>Instantias ad Aquam: Named after the *clepsydra* or water-clock used by the Greeks and Romans.</term>; taking the name from the **Water-clocks** used by the Ancients, into which water was poured instead of sand. These measure **Nature** by **Moments of Time**, just as the **Instances of the Rod** <term>Instantiæ Virgæ: Examples that measure the physical distance or spatial reach of a force.</term> measure by degrees of space. For every motion or natural action is carried out in time; some faster, others slower, but always in specific moments known to Nature. Even those actions which seem to work suddenly, and (as we say) in the blink of an eye, are found to admit of "more and less" in terms of time.

First, therefore, we see that the **revolutions** <note>original: *Restitutiones*; literally "restorations," referring to the time a planet takes to return to the same point in its orbit.</note> of the **Heavenly Bodies** occur through numbered times; as do the **Ebb and Flow of the Sea**. The downward motion of **Heavy things** toward the Earth, and of **Light things** toward the reach of the Heavens, occurs through certain moments, according to the ratio of the body being moved and the medium <note>The substance, such as air or water, through which the object is falling or rising.</note>. Furthermore, the sailing of ships, the motions of animals, and the flight of projectiles all occur likewise through times that are (as far as the totals go) countable. As for **Heat**, we see boys in winter "wash" their hands in a flame; <note>Bacon refers to the feat of passing one's hands quickly through a fire without being burned, demonstrating that the *duration* of exposure determines the effect.</note>

# VERULAMII

...**Gunpowder** <note>original: "Pulvis pyrius"</note> is placed; where immense masses of earth, buildings, and the like are overturned and thrown high into the air by a tiny quantity of gunpowder. The certain cause of this is that the **Motion of Expansion** <note>original: "Motus Dilatationis"</note> of the powder which drives the explosion is many times swifter than the **Motion of Gravity** <note>original: "Motus Gravitatis"</note> by which any resistance could be offered; so much so that the first motion is finished before the opposing motion has even begun, so that at the start there is a kind of "nullity" of resistance. This is also why, in every projectile, a blow that is not so much strong as it is sharp and fast is most effective for piercing through.

# THE WORKS OF BARON VERULAM #

...no forces can reduce even the smallest portion of **Matter** into **Nothing**, but that it remains **Something**, and occupies some **Place**, and (in whatever necessity it is placed) frees itself either by changing its **Form** or its **Location**; or, (if no opportunity is given), it subsists as it is; nor does a thing ever come to the point where it is either **Nothing** or **Nowhere**. This **Motion** the **School** <note>The "School" refers to Scholasticism, the medieval system of philosophy and theology based on Aristotle that Bacon frequently critiques for being too abstract.</note> (which almost always names and defines **Things** by their **Effects** and **Inconveniences** rather than by **Internal Causes**) denotes by that **Axiom**, that *Two bodies cannot be in one place*; or calls it the **Motion** *Lest there be a penetration of dimensions* <note>original: "Ne fiat penetratio dimensionum". This is the principle of impenetrability: the idea that two physical objects cannot occupy the exact same space at the same time.</note>. It is not necessary to provide examples of this **Motion**: for it is inherent in every **Body**.

Let the second **Motion** be the **Motion** (which we call) of **Connection** <term>Connection: original "Nexus"; the force that keeps matter continuous and prevents gaps.</term>, by which **Bodies** do not allow themselves to be separated at any part from contact with another **Body**, as if they enjoy mutual connection and contact. This **Motion** the **School** calls the Motion *Lest a vacuum be created* <note>original: "Ne detur vacuum". Bacon is describing the classical belief that nature "abhors a vacuum" and will move matter to prevent empty space from forming.</note>: such as when water is drawn upward by suction, or through pipes; flesh by **cupping-glasses** <note>Medical jars used to create suction on the skin.</note>; or when water stays put and does not flow out of perforated jars unless the mouth of the jar is opened to let in air; and countless other examples of that kind.

## OF VERULAM ##

The motion of **Resistance** <term>Resistance: original "Antitypiæ"; from the Greek *antitypia*, the quality of matter that prevents two bodies from occupying the same space.</term> and **Connection** <term>Connection: original "Nexus"; the tendency of matter to stay joined and resist being pulled apart.</term>; namely, the release from pressure, associated with the **Motion of Resistance**; and the release from tension, associated with the **Motion of Connection**: as if bodies under pressure would yield or expand themselves only to prevent the **Penetration of Dimensions** <note>original: "Penetratio dimensionum"; the Aristotelian concept that two bodies cannot occupy the same space at the same time.</note>; and as if bodies under tension would snap back and contract only to prevent a **Vacuum**. 

Yet, if compressed air wished to return to the density of water, or wood to the density of stone, there would be no need for the **penetration of dimensions**; and nevertheless, their compression could be far greater than they suffer in any way. In the same manner, if water wished to expand itself into the thinness of air, or stone into the thinness of wood, there would be no need for a vacuum; and yet, their expansion could become far greater than they suffer in any way. 

Therefore, the matter is not reduced to the **Penetration of Dimensions** and the **Vacuum**, except at the ultimate limits of **Condensation** and **Rarefaction**: whereas these motions stop and operate far short of those limits; nor are they anything other than the **Desires of Bodies** to preserve themselves in their own **Consistencies** (or, if they prefer, in their own **Forms** 
<margin>c</margin>
), and not to depart from them suddenly, unless they are altered through gentle means and by mutual consent. 

But it is far more necessary (because it brings much with it) that it be made known to men that **Violent Motion** (which we call **Mechanical**, and which **Democritus** 
<margin>c {</margin>
—who, in explaining his primary motions, is to be ranked even below mediocre philosophers—called the **Motion of the Blow** <note>original: "Motum Plagæ"; referring to the impact or collision of atoms.</note>) is nothing other than the **Motion of Liberty**, namely from compression to **re-** <note>catchword: la- (laxationem); relaxation or release.</note>

<summary>Bacon argues that matter's resistance to compression and tension is a natural "desire" to maintain its consistency rather than a mere avoidance of a vacuum. He reinterprets "Violent Motion" (mechanical force) as the "Motion of Liberty," where matter struggles to return to its original state after being disturbed.</summary>

relaxation. For in every instance, whether it be a simple **pushing forward** or **flight through the air**, no removal or local motion occurs before the parts of the body are unnaturally affected and compressed by the force of the striker. Then, as the parts push one another in succession, the whole is carried along; and not only by moving forward, but also by **rotating** at the same time; so that in this way also the parts can free themselves or endure the pressure more evenly. And so much for this motion.

Let the fourth motion be that which we have named the **Motion of Matter** <term>Motion of Matter: original "Motus Hyles"; from the Greek *hyle* (matter), referring to the expansion or contraction of matter due to its own internal state or external influences like heat.</term>: which is, in a way, the opposite motion to the one we just discussed, the **Motion of Liberty**. For in the **Motion of Liberty**, bodies shrink from, reject, and flee from a new dimension, or a new sphere, or a new expansion or contraction (for these various words imply the same thing), and they strive with all their might to spring back and recover their old consistency. But on the contrary, in this **Motion of Matter**, bodies desire a new sphere or dimension; and they aspire to it willingly and quickly, and sometimes with the most violent effort (as in the case of **Gunpowder** <note>original: "Pulvere Pyrio"; literally "fire-powder."</note>). 

The instruments of this motion—not the only ones certainly, but the most powerful or at least the most frequent—are **Heat** and **Cold**. For example: **Air**, if it is dilated through **Tension** <note>original: "Tensuram"; the act of stretching or expanding.</note> (as by suction in **glass eggs** <note>Early modern scientific instruments, often used in experiments involving air pressure or heat; they were oval-shaped glass vessels.</note>), suffers from a great desire to restore itself. But if heat is applied, on the contrary, it desires to expand, and craves a new sphere, and passes and migrates into it willingly,

Let the ninth motion be **Magnetic Motion**, which, although it belongs to the genus of the *Motion of Minor Congregation*, yet if it operates at great distances and upon great masses of things, it deserves a separate investigation; especially if it neither begins with Contact (as most do), nor brings the action all the way to Contact (as all congregative motions do), but only raises bodies, or causes them to swell up, and nothing more. For if the **Moon** raises the waters, or causes moist things to bulge or swell; or if the **Starry Heaven** attracts the planets toward their apogees <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note>; or if the **Sun** binds the stars of Venus and Mercury so they stay no further from its body than a certain distance; these motions seem to be placed correctly neither under the *Major Congregation* <note>Bacon's term for the general gathering of matter toward the center of the Earth (gravity).</note> nor under the *Minor Congregation*, but are like intermediate and imperfect congregative motions, and therefore ought to constitute a species of their own.

<meta>This page continues Francis Bacon’s systematic classification of the "motions" or fundamental tendencies of matter. Having previously discussed "Minor Congregation" (the attraction of like to like) and "Magnetic Motion," he now introduces its opposite: the motion of repulsion or "flight."</meta>

<page-num>301</page-num>

-># NEW ORGANON #<-

Let the tenth motion be the **Motion of Flight** <note>original: "motus Fugæ." This refers to natural repulsion between substances.</note>; a motion, that is, which is the opposite of the *Motion of Minor Congregation*. By this motion, bodies flee from and drive away hostile things through **antipathy** <term>antipathy: a natural "dislike" or repulsion between two substances that prevents them from mixing</term>, separating themselves from them or refusing to mix with them. For although it may seem in some cases that this motion is only accidental—a consequence of the *Motion of Minor Congregation* (since **homogeneous** <term>homogeneous: substances of the same kind</term> things cannot come together unless **heterogeneous** <term>heterogeneous: substances of a different kind</term> things are excluded and removed)—nevertheless, this motion should be classified as its own distinct type. This is because in many things, the "appetite for flight" is seen to be more primary than the "appetite for union."

This motion stands out remarkably in the **excretions of animals**; and no less in the offensive objects of some of the senses, especially in smell and taste. For a foul odor is so rejected by the sense of smell that it even induces a motion of expulsion in the "mouth of the stomach" <note>The cardia, or the opening where the esophagus meets the stomach.</note> by **sympathy** <note>original: "consensum." In early medicine, this described how one organ reacts to a stimulus in another.</note>; a bitter and harsh taste is so rejected by the palate or throat that it induces a shaking of the head and a shudder by sympathy. 

Furthermore, this motion also has a place in other phenomena. It is observed in certain instances of **antiperistasis** <term>antiperistasis: a theory in ancient physics where a quality intensifies when surrounded by its opposite, such as a cold environment causing heat to "huddle together" and become more intense</term>. For example, in the **middle region of the air** <note>Early modern science divided the atmosphere into layers; the middle region was thought to be perpetually cold because the heat of the sun was reflected from the earth below and the celestial fire was above it.</note>, the cold temperatures seem to be "rejections" of the nature of cold from the borders of the heavenly bodies. Likewise, those great heats and inflammations found in subterranean places seem to be rejections of the nature of heat from the interior of the Earth. For Heat and Cold, if they exist in a smaller quantity...

### NEW ORGANON ###

Let the twelfth motion be the **Motion of Excitation**; which motion seems to be of the genus of ***Assimilation***, and by that name is sometimes used by us interchangeably. For it is a diffusive, communicative, transitive, and multiplicative motion, just like that one; and in effect (for the most part) they agree, although they differ in their mode of effect and in their subject. For the motion of ***Assimilation*** proceeds as if by command and authority; for it orders and forces the assimilated thing to be turned and changed into the assimilator. But the motion of **Excitation** proceeds as if by art and insinuation, and stealthily; and it only invites and disposes the excited thing toward the nature of the exciter. Furthermore, the motion of ***Assimilation*** multiplies and transforms bodies and substances; for instance, more flame is made, more air, more spirit, more flesh. But in the motion of **Excitation**, only virtues <note>original: "virtutes," meaning the inherent powers, qualities, or properties of a thing.</note> are multiplied and passed on; and more heat is made, more magnetism, more putrefaction. This motion is especially prominent in heat and cold. For heat does not diffuse itself in the act of heating through the communication of the original heat <note>that is, by transferring a "fluid" of heat</note>; but only through the ***Excitation*** of the body to that motion which is the **form of heat**; regarding which we spoke in the **First Vintage** <note>original: "Vindemiatione prima." This is Bacon's term for a preliminary conclusion or "first harvest" of results from his inductive process.</note> on the **Nature of Heat**. Therefore, heat is excited much more slowly and with more difficulty in a stone or metal than in air, because of the inability and unreadiness of those bodies for that motion; so that it is likely that there may be materials deeper within the bowels of the Earth which altogether re-

Let the thirteenth motion be the **Motion of Impression**; which motion is also of the genus of the ***Motion of Assimilation***, and it is the most subtle among the diffusive motions. However, it has seemed best to us to categorize it as its own species because of the notable difference it has compared to the previous two. For the simple **Motion of Assimilation** transforms the bodies themselves, so that if you remove the original Mover, it makes no difference to what follows. For this reason, we have become accustomed to calling those motions of **Assimilation** and **Excitation** the **motion of the Generation of Jupiter**, because the generation remains; but this motion [of Impression], we call the **motion of the Generation of Saturn**, because as soon as it is born it is devoured and absorbed <note>Bacon uses Roman mythology here: Jupiter’s reign was stable and lasting, whereas Saturn (Cronus) famously devoured his children as soon as they were born, representing the fleeting nature of this motion.</note>.

This motion truly manifests itself in three things: in rays of light, in the percussions of sounds, and in magnetic properties, insofar as communication is concerned. For when the light is removed, colors and its other images immediately perish; when the first percussion and the shaking of the body caused by it are removed, the sound perishes shortly thereafter. For although sounds are also agitated in a medium through winds as if through waves, nevertheless it must be more carefully noted that the sound does not last as long as the resonance occurs. For when a bell <term>Campana</term> is struck, the sound seems to be continued for a good long time; from which one might easily fall into error by thinking that during all that time the sound was, as it were, swimming and hanging in the air—which is most false. For that resonance <term>Resonatio</term> is not numerically the same sound, but is constantly renewed. This is manifested by the calming or restraint of the struck body. For if the bell is stopped and held firmly so that it becomes immobile, the sound immediately perishes and resonates no longer. The same is seen in strings; if after the first percussion the string is touched, either with a finger, as in a **Lyre**, or with a quill <note>original: "calamo," referring to the plectrum or reed mechanism</note>, as in **Spinets** <note>An early keyboard instrument related to the harpsichord.</note>, the resonance immediately ends. ...seek embraces. For it seems that **Bodies** either move without limit; or rest entirely; or are carried to a boundary where, according to their **Nature**, they either rotate or rest. And those things that are well-placed, if they enjoy **Motion**, move in a **Circle**: that is, in a motion eternal and infinite. Those things that are well-placed and shrink from motion, rest entirely. Those things that are not well-placed move in a **straight line** (as if by the shortest path) to join with their **Kindred Substances** <note>original: "suorum Connaturalium," referring to the theory that matter seeks out other matter of the same type</note>.

Now, this **Motion of Rotation** <term>Spontaneous Rotation: the 17th of Bacon's 24 motions, describing how bodies revolve around a center</term> admits of nine variations <note>original: "Differentias," or distinguishing characteristics</note>.

**First**, of its **Center**, around which the bodies move.
**Second**, of its **Poles**, upon which they move.
**Third**, of its **Circumference** or **Orbit**, according to their distance from the Center.
**Fourth**, of its **Speed** <note>original: "Incitationis"</note>, according as they rotate faster or slower.
**Fifth**, of the **Direction** of its motion, such as from East to West, or from West to East.
**Sixth**, of its **Deviation** from a perfect circle by means of **Spirals** <note>original: "Spiras"; Bacon is likely considering the complex paths planets seem to take, which he often described as spiral-like rather than perfect concentric circles</note> at a greater or lesser distance from their Center.
**Seventh**, of its **Deviation** from a perfect circle by means of spirals at a greater or lesser distance from their **Poles**.
**Eighth**, of the greater or lesser **Distance** of these spirals from one another.
**Ninth** and last, of the **Variation** of the **Poles** themselves, if they are movable; which itself does not belong to rotation unless it occurs in a circular manner.

And this motion, by common and long-standing opinion, is held to be the proper characteristic of **Heavenly Bodies** <note>original: "Cælestium"</note>. Through this **Appetite** <note>original: "Appetitum"; Bacon uses this term to describe the inherent "desires" or natural tendencies of physical matter</note>, all things that are highly **Condensed** shrink from motion; for them, their primary desire is not to move. And though they may be prodded and provoked toward **Motion** in infinite ways, they still protect their **Nature** as much as they can. If they are compelled to move, they always seem to act in such a way as to recover their rest and status, and to move no further. In this effort, they certainly show themselves to be agile, struggling quite nimbly and rapidly (as if weary and impatient of any delay) to return to a state of stillness. However, an image of this appetite can only be seen in part; because here among us, due to the influence and **Concoction of the Heavens** <term>Concoction: In early science, this referred to the "digesting" or refining of matter through heat. Bacon suggests celestial heat keeps earthly matter from reaching its most dense, "restful" state</term>, all **Tangible** <note>original: "Tangibile"; refers to physical, solid matter</note> objects are not only not condensed to their ultimate limit, but are also mixed with some amount of **Spirit** <note>original: "Spiritu"; for Bacon, this is a thin, active substance hidden within all tangible bodies</note>.

We have now proposed the **Species**, or simple **Elements** of the **Motions**, **Appetites**, and **Active Virtues** <note>original: "Virtutum Activarum"</note> which are most **Universal** <note>original: "Catholica," meaning general or applicable to all nature</note> in Nature. And no small part of **Natural Science** is outlined beneath them. We do not deny, however, that other Species might perhaps be added; or that these very divisions could be reorganized according to the truer veins of things; and finally, that they could be reduced to a smaller number. Yet we do not mean this regarding some abstract divisions: as if someone were to say that **Bodies** desire either **Conservation**, or **Exaltation**, or **Propagation**, or the **Enjoyment** of their nature; or if someone...

# THE BARON OF VERULAM #

...[one might] say that the motions of things tend toward **Conservation** <note>original: "Conservationem"</note> and the Good; either of the universe, such as **Resistance** <term>Resistance: Bacon uses the Greek-derived term "Antitypia" to describe the quality by which one body refuses to let another occupy its space</term> and **Connection** <note>original: "Nexum"; the force that prevents a vacuum by keeping matter together</note>; or of large collections, such as the motion of the **Greater Congregation** <note>original: "Congregationis Majoris"; this refers to the attraction of bodies toward the mass of the Earth, similar to gravity</note>, of **Rotation**, and of **Abhorrence of Motion**; or of special Forms, such as the rest. # NOVUM ORGANUM #

...it is sufficiently clear to us from the most powerful **Virtues of Pneumatic Bodies** <note>original: "Corporum Pneumaticorum Virtutibus"; refers to the active powers of gases, vapors, or "spirits" within matter</note>, (which otherwise would float like minute dust particles in a **Vacuum**) and from many other demonstrations. The remaining **Motions**, however, rule and are ruled in turn, according to the ratios of their Strength, Quantity, Speed, and Projection, as well as the Aids and Obstacles they encounter.

For example: a certain armed magnet holds and suspends iron up to sixty times its own weight; in that case, the **Motion of the Lesser Congregation** <term>Motion of the Lesser Congregation: The internal attraction between specific bodies, such as magnetism or local cohesion</term> dominates over the **Motion of the Greater Congregation** <note>original: "Motus Congregationis Majoris"; gravity, or the tendency of heavy objects to fall toward the Earth</note>. But if the weight is increased beyond that, it yields. If sulfur alone is put into a handgun with a ball and fire is applied, the ball is not discharged; in that instance, the **Motion of the Greater Congregation** overcomes the **Motion of Matter** <note>original: "Motus Hyles"; likely referring here to the expansive power inherent in the material’s density or "bulk" when heated</note>. But when **Gunpowder** is used, it overcomes the **Motion of Matter** in the sulfur, aided by the **Motions of Matter** and of **Flight** <term>Motion of Flight: A repulsive force where parts of a substance seek to escape from one another, as seen in explosions</term> within the niter <note>saltpeter</note>. # VERULAM #

...and so it is for the rest. For the **Instances of Strife** <term>Instances of Strife: Cases where one natural force or "motion" overcomes another; Bacon also calls these "Wrestling Instances"</term> (which indicate the **Predominance of Powers** <note>original: "Prædominantiam Virtutum"; refers to the active forces or qualities inherent in matter</note>, and according to what ratios and calculations they prevail or yield) must be sought out from all sides with sharp and diligent care.

The methods and reasons why these motions yield must also be carefully examined. Namely, do they cease entirely, or do they rather continue to push but are restrained? For in the bodies here around us, there is no such thing as true Rest, neither in the whole nor in the parts; it exists only in appearance. This apparent rest is caused either by **Equilibrium** <note>original: "Æquilibrium"</note> or by the absolute **Predominance of Motions**. By **Equilibrium**, as in scales, which stand still if the weights are equal. By **Predominance**, as in perforated jars <note>original: "Hydriis perforatis"; reference to a vessel that holds water against gravity as long as no air can enter, often used to demonstrate the "Motion of Connection"</note>, where the water remains at rest and is kept from falling by the **Predominance of the Motion of Connection** <term>Motion of Connection: The force that keeps matter together to prevent a vacuum from forming</term>.

It should be noted, however (as we have said), to what extent those yielding motions continue to exert force. For if someone is held pinned to the ground in a struggle, with arms and legs bound or otherwise restrained, and yet they still strive with all their strength to rise again; that **Exertion** <note>original: "Nixus"</note> is no less real, even though it does not succeed. The condition of this matter—namely, whether by **Predominance** the **Yielding Motion** is as if annihilated, or whether the **Exertion** continues though it is not seen—which remains hidden during conflicts, will perhaps become visible when forces act together.

And men have been led to this opinion by those common **Experiments** of an **inverted Cup** over **Water** with a lighted **Candle** or **Paper**; from which it happens that the **Water** is drawn upwards; and similarly of **Cupping Glasses** <term>Ventosæ: medical instruments used to create suction on the skin, often for bloodletting</term>, which, being heated over a flame, draw the flesh. Regarding the **Second Mode** of the seven aforementioned, it must first be noted that **Compressions** and similar **Violent Forces** <note>original: "Violentias" — in Aristotelian physics, "violent" motion is that which is imposed by an external force, contrary to a thing's "natural" tendency</note> are certainly most powerful for local **Motion** and other things of that kind, as seen in **Machines** and **Missiles**; they are also powerful for the destruction of an **Organic Body** and those **Virtues** <term>Virtutum: the inherent powers, capacities, or functional properties of a substance</term> which consist plainly in **Motion**. # NOVUM ORGANUM.

...given [qualities], they might become constant and fixed, and as if changed into **Nature**. This should first be tested through simple **Delay** <term>Mora: the passage of time or duration allowed for a process to take hold</term>; then through **Aids** and **Agreements** <note>original: "Consensus" — Bacon’s term for the natural sympathies or "agreements" between different substances that allow them to work together</note>. And this would have been ready for us (if only it had come to mind) when we condensed **Water** (which is discussed elsewhere) through hammerings and presses, before it burst out. For we ought to have left the flattened **Sphere** <note>Bacon refers to his famous experiment where he filled a leaden globe with water and crushed it to see if water could be compressed</note> to itself for several days, and only then extracted the **Water**; so that an **Experiment** might be made, to see whether it would have immediately filled such a dimension as it had before **Condensation**.

If it had not done so either immediately, or at least shortly after, then that **Condensation** could clearly have been seen as having become permanent. If not, it would have appeared that a **Restoration** <note>original: "Restitutionem" — the act of a substance "springing back" or returning to its original state, similar to elasticity</note> had occurred, and the **Compression** had been transitory. Something similar should also have been done regarding the **Extension** of **Air** in **Glass Eggs** <term>Ova vitrea: egg-shaped glass flasks used in early modern chemistry and physics experiments</term>. For after a strong suction, a sudden and firm **Closing** <note>original: "Obturatio" — the sealing or corking of a vessel</note> ought to have been performed; then those **Eggs** ought to have remained so sealed for several days; and only then should it have been tested whether, upon opening the hole, **Air** would have been drawn in with a hiss, or even if as great a quantity of **Water** would have been drawn in after immersion as would have been at the beginning, if no delay had been applied.

For it is probable, or at least worthy of proof, that these things could have been and can be done; because in **Bodies** that are slightly more dissimilar <note>meaning substances that are more solid or less uniform than air or water</note>, the **Duration of Time** effects similar things. For a **Stick** bent by **Compression** does not spring back after some time;

There are two **Modes of Condensation** of the **Spirits** by **Soporific** medicines (or those that provoke **Sleep**): one by the **Calming of Motion**; the other by the **Flight of the Spirits**. 

Indeed, **Violet**, **dried Rose**, **Lettuce**, and such "blessed" or benign substances, through their friendly and moderately cooling vapors, invite the **Spirits** to unite themselves, and they restrain their sharp and restless **Motion**. But **Opiates** and their relatives plainly drive the **Spirits** away, by their malignant and hostile quality. Therefore, if they are applied to an external part, the **Spirits** immediately flee from that part, and no longer willingly flow into it. If, however, they are taken internally, their vapors—ascending to the **Head**—drive out the **Spirits** contained within the **Ventricles of the Brain** from every side. And as the **Spirits** withdraw themselves, and are unable to escape into any other part, they consequently come together and are **condensed**; and sometimes they are plainly extinguished and suffocated. However, the *works* of gentler heat should have been attempted and investigated, from which more subtle *mixtures* and ordered *schematisms* could be produced and brought forth, following the *example of Nature* and the *imitation of the sun's works*; just as we sketched out in the *aphorism* on *Instances of Alliance* <note>original: "Instantiis Foederis"</note>. ### NOVUM ORGANUM
## 331

But above all, the **Inquiry** and **Discovery** of the **Effects** and **Operations** of heat—as it **Approaches** and **Recedes**, gradually, in an orderly way, periodically, and through proper intervals and delays—must be attempted. For this **ordered inequality** <note>original: "Inæqualitas ordinata"</note> is truly the **Daughter of Heaven** and the **Mother of Generation**. No great thing should be expected from heat that is either violent, or sudden, or surging. Indeed, this is most evident in the growth of plants. Furthermore, in the **Wombs of Animals**, there is a great **Inequality of heat**, resulting from the motion, sleep, feeding, and passions of the females who carry the womb. Finally, in the very **Matrices of the Earth** <note>original: "Matricibus Terræ"</note>—those in which **Metals** and **Minerals** are formed—this inequality has its place and flourishes. This makes the ignorance of certain **Reformed Alchemists** <term>Reformed Alchemists: Likely a reference to followers of Paracelsus or other contemporary "chemists" who sought to improve alchemical theory but still relied on simplistic methods</term> all the more notable; they believed they would achieve their desires through the uniform heats of lamps and similar devices that burn steadily in a single, unchanging tenor. So much, then, for the **Operations** and **Effects** of heat. However, it is not yet the right time to examine these thoroughly, before the **Forms of Things** and the **Schemas of bodies** have been further investigated and brought to light. For instruments are to be sought, applied, and adapted only when we are certain about the **Models** <note>original: "Exemplaribus"</note> we are following.

The **Fourth Mode** of operating is by **Delay** <note>original: "Mora"</note>, which is surely the **Steward and Butler** <term>Steward and Butler: "Promus & Condus," a Latin idiom referring to the servants in a Roman household who managed the stores, one bringing items out for use and the other putting them away</term> of **Nature**, and a kind of **Dispensatrix**. <header>OF VERULAM</header>

...[things being] notable, protected and defended meanwhile from any external force. For it is then that **internal motions** <note>original: "Motus intestini"; Bacon refers to the inherent, natural movements of particles within a substance</note> reveal and perfect themselves, when external and foreign motions cease. Furthermore, the works of **Age** <note>original: "Ætatis"; here meaning the passage of time</note> are far more subtle than those of **Fire**. For such a clarification of wine cannot be achieved by Fire as is achieved by **Delay** <note>original: "Moram"; the deliberate use of time to allow natural processes to occur</note>; nor are incinerations by Fire as refined as the **dissolutions** and **consumptions** that occur over centuries. 

Also, the incorporations and **mixtures** that are sudden and rushed by Fire are far inferior to those produced by Delay. However, the dissimilar and various **Structural Arrangements** <note>original: "Schematismi"; Bacon's term for the internal "schemes" or configurations of matter</note> which bodies attempt through Delay (such as rot or putrefaction) are destroyed by Fire or more intense heat. Meanwhile, it is worth noting that the motion of bodies that are completely enclosed has something of the **violent** about it. For that "imprisonment" hinders the spontaneous motions of the body. 

Therefore, Delay in an **open vessel** contributes more to **Separations**; in a **completely closed vessel**, it leads to **Mixtures**; in a **partially closed vessel** where air can still enter, it leads to **Putrefactions**. In any case, examples of the works and effects of Delay must be diligently sought from every source.

But the **Control of Motion** <note>original: "Regimen Motus"</note> (which is the fifth of the **Modes of Operation** <term>Modes of Operation: The different ways a researcher can manipulate nature to produce effects</term>) is of no small importance. We call it "Control of Motion" when one body, moving spontaneously and meeting another, hinders, repels, admits, or directs the motion of that second body. This truly depends for the most part on the **Shapes and Positions of Vessels**. For an upright cone assists in con-

# NOVUM ORGANUM.

...the condensation of Vapors in **Stills** <note>original: "Alembicis"; an alembic was a classic piece of distilling equipment used to cool and condense liquid.</note>; while an **inverted cone** helps in the **Refining** <note>original: "Defæcationem"; the process of removing dregs or impurities.</note> of **Sugar** in overturned vessels. Sometimes, however, a **winding path** is required, or a **narrowing**, or alternating with **expansion**, and the like. Also, all **Filtration** <note>original: "Percolatio".</note> belongs to this category; namely, when an encountering body opens a path for one part of another body while blocking it for another. 

Nor does **Filtration** or any other **Control of Motion** <note>original: "Regimen Motus"; the deliberate guiding of how particles or substances move.</note> always happen from the outside: it also occurs through a body within a body. This is seen when **small stones** are placed in water to collect their muddiness; or when **Syrups** are clarified with **Egg Whites**, so that the coarser parts stick to the whites and can later be separated. 

Furthermore, **Telesio** <note>Bernardino Telesio (1509–1588), an Italian natural philosopher who emphasized sensory experience but whom Bacon often criticized for being too speculative.</note> quite lightly and ignorantly attributed the **Forms of Animals** to this Control of Motion, claiming they were shaped by the channels and cavities of the womb. He ought, however, to have noted a similar shaping in **Eggshells**, where there are no folds or irregularities. Yet it is true that the Control of Motion completes certain shapes in **molds** and **prototypes**.

But operations performed through **Agreements or Avoidances** <note>original: "Consensus aut Fugas"; the sixth Mode of Operation, referring to what modern science might call chemical affinities or repulsions.</note> (which is the **sixth Mode**) often lie hidden in the depths. For those so-called **Hidden Properties**, and **Specific Virtues**, and **Sympathies**, and **Antipathies**, are for the most part corruptions of philosophy. Nor is there much hope for discovering the agreements of things before the discovery of **Forms** and simple **Structures** <note>original: "Schematismorum"; Bacon’s term for the internal configurations or patterns of matter.</note>. For **Agreement** <note>original: "Consensus".</note> is nothing other than the **Symmetry** of Forms and Structures with one another.

-> OF VERULAM <-

However, the major and more **universal agreements** <note>original: "catholici rerum consensus"; Bacon uses "catholic" in the sense of general or broad, referring to laws that apply across the whole of nature.</note> of things are not entirely obscure. Therefore, we must begin with them. Their first and highest distinction is this: that certain bodies differ greatly in their **Abundance and Rarity of Matter** <note>original: "Copia & Raritate Materiae"; essentially what we would call mass and volume, or the relative "stuff" vs "space" in a substance.</note>, yet agree in their **Configuration** <term>Schematismus: Bacon's term for the internal structure or specific arrangement of parts within a substance.</term>; others, on the contrary, agree in Abundance and Rarity of Matter, but differ in Configuration.

For it was not badly noted by the **Chemists** <note>original: "Chymicis"; Bacon refers here to the followers of Paracelsus, who believed all matter was composed of three primary principles: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note> in their **Triad of principles**, that **Sulfur** and **Mercury** permeate, as it were, the whole universe of things. (For the reasoning regarding **Salt** is foolish, but it was introduced so that it might include earthy, dry, and fixed bodies.) Yet certainly in those two [Sulfur and Mercury], a certain **Agreement of Nature** among the most universal ones is seen. Indeed, **Sulfur**, **Oil** and greasy **Exhalation**, **Flame**, and perhaps the **Body of a Star** all agree. On the other side, **Mercury**, **Water** and **Watery Vapors**, **Air**, and perhaps pure and **interstellar Ether** all agree. 

Nevertheless, these **twin Quaternions** <note>Groups of four.</note>, or **Great Tribes** of things (each within its own order), differ immensely in Abundance of Matter and **Density**, but they strongly agree in Configuration: as they reveal themselves in many ways. But on the other hand, different **Metals** agree much in Abundance and Density (especially compared to plants, etc.), but they differ in Configuration in many ways; and similarly, various **Plants** and **Animals** are varied by almost infinite Configurations, yet they are contained within an Abundance of Matter, or Density, of only a few degrees.

### NEW ORGANON

Next follows an **Agreement** <note>original: "Consensus"; here meaning the natural sympathies or functional relationships between different parts of nature.</note> which is most universal after the previous one: namely, that of **principal bodies and their sources**; that is, of **solvents** <term>menstrua: In alchemy and early chemistry, a "menstruum" was a solvent used to dissolve solids or extract essences.</term> and **nutriments**. 

Therefore, it must be investigated under which climates, in what kind of earth, and at what depth individual **metals** are generated. Similarly, we must study **gems**, whether they are born from rocks or within mines: in which clod of earth individual trees, shrubs, and herbs most commonly grow and, as it were, "rejoice." We should also investigate which **fertilizers** <note>original: "impinguationes"; literally the "fattening" of the soil.</note> provide the most help—whether through dung of any kind, or through chalk, sea sand, ashes, and so on—and which of these are more suitable and beneficial for different varieties of soil. 

Also, the **grafting and budding** <note>original: "insitio & inoculatio"; two methods of propagating plants by joining tissues from one to another.</note> of trees and plants, and the logic behind them—specifically which plants are more successfully grafted onto others—depends greatly upon these **Affinities**. In this regard, it would be quite a pleasant experiment to try something we recently heard was attempted: the grafting of **wild trees** (an operation which has until now usually been restricted to garden trees). By this method, it is said that leaves and acorns are greatly enlarged, and the trees become more shade-giving.

...tolerable, it has almost vanished. We must also take note of the various types of **decaying matter** <term>putrefactions: In the 17th century, it was widely believed that "putrefaction" or organic decay was a creative process that spontaneously generated small organisms.</term> from which **tiny living creatures** <note>original: "Animalcula"</note> are generated.

And the **Agreements** <note>original: "Consensus"; the natural harmonious relationships or "fit" between things.</note> of principal bodies toward their subordinate parts (for those we have mentioned can be seen as such) are quite obvious. To these, we can add the agreements of the **senses toward their objects**. Since these agreements are most evident, if they are well-noted and sharply examined, they could provide great light for understanding other agreements that are currently hidden.

However, the **internal agreements and avoidances** <note>original: "Consensus & Fugæ"</note> of bodies—which we might call their **friendships and quarrels**—are very rarely understood. We are almost weary of the terms "sympathy" and "antipathy" because of the superstitions and empty talk usually associated with them. These relationships are often falsely identified, filled with fables, or simply neglected. 

For example, if someone claims there is a **discord between a vine and a cabbage** <note>The Roman author Pliny the Elder famously claimed that vines would shrink away from cabbages planted nearby.</note> because they do not grow well when planted together, the reason is actually simple: both plants are succulent and **predatory** <note>original: "deprædatrix"; meaning they aggressively strip the soil of nutrients.</note> regarding their nutrition, so one robs the other. Or, if someone claims there is an "agreement and friendship" between **grain crops** and the **cornflower** <note>original: "Cyaneum"</note> or the **wild poppy**, because those flowers almost never appear except in cultivated fields, they should instead claim there is a discord. The poppy and cornflower are actually produced from the specific "juices" of the earth that the grain has rejected or left behind; thus, the sowing of the grain merely prepares the soil for their later appearance. There is a great number of such false attributions. As for fables, indeed...

# OF NATURAL HISTORY,
## AND EXPERIMENTAL,

->Such as may suffice, and be in order to the Base, and Foundations of true Philosophy.<-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing floral patterns and foliage in a square frame.</image-desc>That we publish our **Great Restoration** <note>original: *Instauratio*; Bacon’s grand project to overhaul all human knowledge.</note> in parts, is done with this aim: that something may be placed beyond the reach of peril <note>Bacon was aware of his own mortality and the political instability of his time; publishing in sections ensured his ideas would survive even if the whole work was never finished.</note>. A similar reason moves us now to subjoin another small portion of the Work, and to publish it along with those things we have already completed. This is the **Description and Delineation of a Natural and Experimental History**, specifically of the kind required to build a true **Philosophy**. It is intended to encompass material that is trustworthy, abundant, and properly arranged for the work of the **Interpreter** <note>The "Interpreter of Nature" is Bacon's term for the researcher who uses his new method of induction to uncover nature's secrets.</note> which follows. 

To be sure, the proper place for this would have been when we reached the **Preparations for Inquiry** <note>original: *Parascevas Inquisitionis*; "Parasceve" is a Greek-derived term meaning preparation, often used in a religious context for the eve of a Sabbath.</note> in the natural order of things. Yet it seems more prudent to us to anticipate this stage rather than wait for its proper place. This is because a History of this kind—as we conceive it and shall soon describe it—is a task of immense **Bulk**. It cannot be accomplished without great labor and expense, for it requires the efforts of many and is (as we have said elsewhere) a work fit for a **King** <note>original: *opus Regium*; Bacon believed that gathering all the facts of the natural world was too big for one man and required state support.</note>. It occurred to us, therefore, that it might be worthwhile to see if these things might perhaps become the concern of others; so that, while we devote ourselves—

## APHORISM.

<margin>I.</margin>
Nature exists in a triple state, and undergoes as it were a threefold governance. For she is either free and unfolds herself in her ordinary course; or she is driven from her proper state by the depravities and insolence of matter and the violence of obstacles; or she is constrained and molded by human art and service. The first state refers to the **species** <term>Species: In this context, the standard, "normal" types of things found in nature, like a typical oak tree or a healthy horse.</term> of things; the second to **monsters** <term>Monsters: From the Latin *monstra*, meaning biological rarities, deformities, or anything that deviates from the "normal" course of nature.</term>; the third to **artificial things**. Indeed, in artificial things, Nature receives a yoke from the empire of man; for these things would never have been made without the aid of humanity. Yet, through the labor and service of man, a completely new face of bodies is seen, appearing like another universe of things, or a second theater. Therefore, **Natural History** <note>In the 17th century, a "History" was not just a record of the past, but a systematic collection of data and observations about a specific subject.</note> is threefold. For it treats either the **Liberty of Nature**, or her **Errors**, or her **Bonds**; so that we may quite properly divide it into the **History of Generations**, **Pretergenerations**, and **Arts**. The last of these we have also been accustomed to call **Mechanical** and **Experimental** history. Nor yet <meta>catchword: it</meta>

# Natural and Experimental [History]

We do not strictly command that these three <note>Original: "hæc tria"—referring to the categories of Species, Monsters, and Arts established on the previous page.</note> be handled separately. For why should the History of Monsters not be joined with the History of the Species themselves in each instance? Even Artificial things <note>Man-made objects or results of human technology.</note> are sometimes rightly joined with the Species, and sometimes better separated. Therefore, it is best to take counsel from the nature of the matter as it arises. For a rigid Method produces repetitions and long-windedness just as much when it is excessive as when it is absent.

II. Natural History, though threefold in its Subject (as we have said), is twofold in its Use. For it is employed either for the knowledge of the things themselves which are recorded in the History, or as the primary matter of Philosophy and the supply—or "Forest" <term>Forest: Translated from the Latin *Sylva*. In early modern science, this referred to a "timber-yard" of facts—raw materials collected for the purpose of building a larger philosophical or scientific structure.</term>—of true Induction <term>Induction: The process of reaching a general conclusion or "law of nature" by observing many specific examples.</term>. It is this latter use that we are concerned with now—now, I say, and never before. For neither **Aristotle**, nor **Theophrastus**, nor **Dioscorides**, nor **Caius Plinius** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), the author of a massive Roman encyclopedia of the natural world.</note>, and much less the moderns, ever proposed this goal (of which we speak) for Natural History. It is of the utmost importance that those who hereafter take up the task of writing Natural History should constantly reflect upon this: they are not serving the reader's pleasure, nor even providing immediate practical benefits from their accounts, but are gathering and comparing a vast Abundance and variety of Things sufficient for constructing true Axioms <term>Axioms: Established principles or laws of nature derived from evidence.</term>. If they keep this in mind, they will determine the proper Method for such a History themselves. For the End governs the Method.

<header>Preparation for History</header>

III. Since this task requires such great effort and labor, it is only right that it should not be burdened with superfluous details. There are, therefore, three things about which men must be clearly warned, so they may invest their effort in them very sparingly; for these things increase the bulk of the Work immensely, but promote its effectiveness little or not at all.

First, let us do away with **Antiquities** <note>Original: *Antiquitates* — historical lore, myths, or ancient fables often included in early science books.</note>, and **Citations**, or the "Votes" of various Authors; likewise, let us remove disputes, controversies, and differing opinions; and finally, everything **Philological** <term>Philological: In this context, it refers to the study of texts, linguistics, and the history of words rather than the study of the physical world itself.</term>. An Author should not be cited unless the matter is of doubtful credibility; nor should a controversy be introduced unless the matter is of great importance. As for those things which pertain to the Ornaments of Speech, metaphors, the "Treasure of Eloquence," and such vanities, they should be cast aside entirely. Even the facts that are accepted should be presented briefly and concisely, so that they are nothing but the barest accounts. For no one who collects and stores materials for Buildings or Ships or similar structures arranges and displays them beautifully (in the manner of a shopkeeper) to please the eye; instead, he is only diligent that they be sound and good, and that they occupy the minimum amount of space in the Warehouse. This is exactly how one must proceed.

Second, that "Luxury" found in many Natural Histories—the countless descriptions and pictures of species and the curious varieties of the same—does not contribute much to the goal. For such tiny variations are nothing other than a "Sport of Nature" <term>Sport of Nature: Translated from the Latin *Lusus Naturę*. A term used by early modern scholars to describe unusual or freakish occurrences in nature that seemed to happen "playfully" or without a clear purpose.</term>, and a kind of playfulness, and they border on Indivi-
