### IV.

In the **History** which we require and intend in our mind, it must be seen above all else that it lies open widely, and is made to the **Measure of the Universe**. For the World must not be narrowed down to the smallness of the Intellect (as has been done until now), but the Intellect must be expanded and loosened to receive the **Image of the World**, just as it is found. For that habit, *to look at a few things and pronounce judgment based on a few things*, has ruined everything. Resuming, therefore, the Division which we made a little while ago of **Natural History** (namely, that it consists of *Generations*, *Pretergenerations*, and *Arts* <note>These represent regular nature, nature "gone wrong" or monsters, and nature modified by human technology.</note>), we establish five Parts for the *History of Generations*. 

Let the first be of the **Ether and Heavenly bodies**. The second, of **Meteors**, and the (so-called) **Regions of the Air**; namely, the tracts from the Moon down to the Surface of the Earth. To this part we also assign **Comets** of every kind, both the higher and lower ones (whatever the truth of the matter may be <note>Bacon acknowledges the contemporary debate over whether comets were atmospheric "meteors" or distant celestial bodies.</note>), for the sake of Order. 

The third, of **Earth and Sea**. The fourth, of the **Elements** (which they call Flame or Fire, Air, Water, and Earth). We wish **Elements** to be understood in this sense: not as the *first beginnings of things* <note>Original: *Primordiis Rerum*. He is distinguishing his use of the word from the philosophical or atomic "building blocks" of matter.</note>, but as the **Greater Masses** of Natural Bodies. For thus the Nature of Things...

We must also resume at this point what we treated more extensively in *Aphorisms* 99, 119, and 120 of *Book One* <note>Referring to the first book of Bacon's *Novum Organum* (1620), where he defends his focus on "low" or "vile" subjects.</note>; here, however, in the manner of a **Precept**, it may suffice to command it briefly: That is, that there be received into this **History**:

*   First, the most **Commonplace** things, which one might think redundant to record because they are so familiarly known;
*   Next, things that are **Vile**, **Illiberal**, and **Base**; (for "all things are pure to the pure" <note>original: *Omnia enim munda mundis*. A quote from the Epistle to Titus 1:15.</note>; and if profit from urine has a good smell <note>original: *Lucrum ex Lotio boni odoris*. A reference to the Roman Emperor Vespasian, who defended a tax on public toilets by saying *pecunia non olet*—"money does not smell." Bacon is saying that knowledge is valuable regardless of its "dirty" source.</note>, much more so do **Light** and **Information** from any matter whatever);
*   Also things that are **Slight** and **Childish**; (and no wonder, for one must plainly become a child again <note>A common theme in Bacon's work is that the scientist must approach nature with the humility and unbiased mind of a child.</note>);
*   Finally, things which seem to be of a certain excessive **Subtlety**, because...

<summary>Bacon argues that a true Natural History must include mundane, "lowly," and common observations—like the salting of meat or the color of bricks—not just to improve trade, but to provide data for the "sea of philosophy." ...in themselves might be of no use. For (as has already been said) the things proposed in this **History** <note>original: *Historia*. To Bacon, a "Natural History" is a vast encyclopedia of facts and observations about the world that serves as the raw material for science.</note> are not gathered for their own sake. Therefore, it is not right to measure their value on their own, but rather by how much they can be applied to other things and flow into **Philosophy**.

VII. Furthermore, we instruct that all things in nature—both **Bodies** and **Powers** <note>original: *Virtutibus*. In this context, "virtues" refers to the inherent forces, qualities, or active powers within matter, such as heat or magnetism.</note>—should (as far as possible) be presented as counted, weighed, measured, and determined. For we are planning **Works**, not **Speculations**. Indeed, **Physics** and **Mathematics**, when well combined, produce **Practice** <note>original: *Practicam*. This refers to applied science or the ability to produce useful results and inventions.</note>. For this reason, we must seek and record the exact **Revolutions** <note>original: *Restitutiones*. Literally "restorations," referring to the period of time it takes for a planet to return to a specific position in the sky.</note> and **Distances** of the planets in the **History of the Heavenly Bodies**; the circumference of the **Earth** and how much area it occupies on the surface relative to the **Waters** in the **History of Earth and Sea**; how much compression the **Air** can suffer without strong **Resistance** <term>Antitypia<gloss>A Greek-derived term used by early scientists to describe "impenetrability" or the resistance matter offers against being compressed or displaced.</gloss></term> in the **History of the Air**; and how much one **Metal** outweighs another in the **History of Metals**. Countless other things of this sort must be investigated and written down. 

However, when exact **Proportions** cannot be obtained, we must certainly resort to estimates or indefinite comparisons. For instance (if by chance we distrust the calculations of **Astronomers** regarding distances), we might state that the **Moon** is below the shadow of the **Earth**; that **Mercury** is above the **Moon**; and things of this kind. Even when middle-ground **Proportions** cannot be found, the extremes should be presented: for example, that a weaker **Magnet** lifts a piece of **Iron** of such-and-she weight in proportion to the weight of the **Stone** itself; and that...

VIII. As for the credibility of those things which are to be accepted into the **History**, it is necessary that they be either of **Certain** faith, **Doubtful** faith, or **Rejected** <note>original: *Damnatae*. Literally "condemned" or dismissed as false.</note> faith. The first kind is to be set forth simply. The second with a note; namely, by the word "**It is reported**," or "**They relate**," or "**I have heard from a trustworthy source**," and the like. For it would be too laborious to write down the arguments for credibility on either side, and it would undoubtedly delay the writer too much. Nor does it matter much for what is being done: since (as we said in **Aphorism 118, Book 1**) unless they abound everywhere, the truth of the **Axioms** <note>original: *Axiomatum*. Furthermore, it will not be beside the point to note the origin of any such **Vanity** or **Credulity**, if it should happen to be discovered. For instance, the herb **Satyrion** <note>original: *Satyrio*. A name for several species of orchids, derived from the Satyrs of myth due to the plant's reputation.</note> has been attributed the power to excite **Sexual Desire** <note>original: *Venerem*. From the Greek word for twins, often used in medicine and botany to refer to paired structures.</note>. It is clear, however, that the new root is always found to be solid and juicy, while the old one is withered and spongy. Therefore, it is no wonder if one sinks in water while the other floats. This is nevertheless regarded as a miracle, and has given further authority to the other supposed powers of that herb.

# Preparation for History

...can be bent and adapted to the work of the **Interpreter**, <note>Bacon’s "Interpreter of Nature" is the philosopher who takes raw data and applies inductive reasoning to discover the laws of science.</note> which follows next. These [rules] are five in number.

**First**, **Questions** (I do not mean questions of **Causes**, <note>original: *Causarum*. In traditional philosophy, "causes" explained the "why"; Bacon insists we first document the "what" (the facts).</note> but of **Fact**) should be added to provoke and invite further investigation. For example, in the *History of Earth and Sea*, one might ask: whether the **Caspian Sea** ebbs and flows, and at what hourly intervals; **Whether** there is some **Southern Continent**, <note>original: *Continens Australis*. In Bacon's time, the existence of a massive southern landmass—Antarctica or a larger "Terra Australis"—was a subject of intense geographical speculation.</note> or rather an **Island**; and similar matters.

**Secondly**, in the case of any new or more subtle experiment, the specific **method** used for that experiment must be included. This is so that people may judge freely for themselves whether the **Information** gained through that experiment is reliable or deceptive, and also so that human ingenuity may be stirred to seek out more accurate methods, if possible.

**Thirdly**, if there is any doubt or hesitation regarding a report, we do not want it suppressed or kept silent at all. Instead, it should be recorded plainly and clearly as a **Note or Warning**. For we desire that this **primary History** be written with the utmost religious care, as if a **Sacrament** <note>original: *Sacramento*. Here used in the sense of a solemn oath of truth-telling.</note> had been sworn regarding its truth in every detail; for it is the **Volume of God's Works** and—insofar as one may compare the Majesty of Divine things with the Humility of Earthly things—it is like a **second Scripture**. <note>original: *Scriptura altera*. Bacon famously argued that God gave us two books: the Book of God's Word (the Bible) and the Book of God's Works (Nature).</note>

**Fourthly**, it will not be out of place to occasionally scatter **Observations** throughout (as **C. Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman author of the encyclopedic *Natural History*.</note> did). For instance, in the *History of Earth and Sea*, one might observe that the shape of the landmasses (so far as they are currently known in relation to the seas) is narrow and [pointed] toward the South...

In this context, these are "rules" or "axioms"—general, universal observations derived from the gathered data.</note> (which are nothing other than general and universal observations) are very effectively added: as in the **History of the Heavens**; <note>original: *Historia Cœlestium*.</note> That **Venus** is never further from the **Sun** than 46 degrees, and **Mercury** no more than 23. Furthermore, another kind of observation should be applied, which has not yet come into use, although it is of no small importance. It is this: namely, that to those things which *are*, those things which *are not* should be subjoined. For instance, in the **History of the Heavens**, that no oblong or triangular star is found; but that every star is globular: either simply globular, like the **Moon**; or angular in appearance, but globular in the center, like the other stars; or "hairy" <note>original: *comata*. This refers to the constellation Auriga (the Charioteer) or the Big Dipper/Wain.</note> etc.); and there is scarcely even a straight line to be found, except perhaps in the **Belt** and **Dagger of Orion**.

<meta>This page concludes Francis Bacon’s "Catalogue of Particular Histories." It follows the previous page's list of technical and mechanical subjects, concluding with mathematics and a summary of his methodology for data collection.</meta>

<page-num>372</page-num>

Histories of pure **Mathematics** must also be written, although they are observations rather than experiments. <note>original: *Historiae conscribendae sunt, licet sint potius Observationes quam Experimenta*; Bacon suggests that while mathematics is abstract, the way numbers and shapes behave in the world should be recorded as a "history" or a database of facts.</note>

129. **History of the natures and powers of Numbers.**

130. **History of the natures and powers of Figures.** <note>original: *Figurarum*; this refers to geometric shapes and spatial forms.</note>

It will not be out of place to mention that, since it is necessary for many experiments to fall under two or more headings (just as the **History of Plants** and the **History of the Art of Gardening** will have many things in common), the **Inquiry** is more conveniently conducted by the **Arts**, while the **Arrangement** is better organized by **Bodies**. <note>Bacon is explaining his taxonomy: it is easier to research topics based on human crafts (Arts), but the final scientific database should be organized by the physical objects themselves (Bodies).</note> For we care little for the mechanical arts themselves, but only for those things they contribute toward the instruction of **Philosophy**. <note>In Bacon's time, "Philosophy" (specifically Natural Philosophy) was the term for what we now call science. He is interested in technology only insofar as it reveals the laws of nature.</note> However, these matters will be better governed as they arise from the work itself.

> <unclear>Eternal life</unclear> itself will be the same for all the saints; an equal **Denarius** <note>original Latin: *æqualis Denarius*; a Roman silver coin. In the Bible, it represents the reward given to laborers in a vineyard regardless of how long they worked.</note> is assigned to all. However, because in that same eternal life the lights of their merits will shine distinctly... one is honored more brightly than another.

Is this not what happens with a **Book**? Bring here the book of Holy Scripture, which we call the **Bible**, and show it to everyone present. A child looks at it and finds his happiness in turning the pages of the illustrations. A printer looks at it and is happy to see the perfection of the characters. A grammarian looks at it and admires its construction. A rhetorician celebrates its eloquence; a historian applauds its beautiful histories; but then a great theologian comes to read it, and he penetrates many mysteries, delighting in the **Wisdom of God** and the admirable works of His power. What is this? Is it not the same Book? It is clear that it is; but the capacity and study of those who read that Book are not the same. Let us linger no longer, but rather let us work in the study of Sacred love <note>The author uses the phrase *amor Sagrado* to suggest that the "eyes" of the heart must be trained to understand divine things.</note> to read with greater clarity the **Book of Bliss**:
